docs.title: psxsplash
docs.text:
psxsplash makes PlayStation 1 games. One download holds the editor, the psxsplash engine and the pcsx-redux emulator: build a scene, press Play, and it boots in the emulator. The same scene runs on a real console over a serial cable, or burns to a disc.

Download the nightly build Get started

docs.title: What you get
docs.text:
• The editor. Scene tree, a viewport that draws the way the console does, an inspector for every object, a project browser, and memory meters for VRAM, SPU RAM and main RAM that update as you work.
  • Two ways to script. Write Lua in the built-in code editor, or snap blocks together in the block editor. Both make the same Lua for the console, and a scene can mix them.
  • The engine. psxsplash runs on the PS1: fixed-point 3D, rooms and portals, navigation, UI canvases, cutscenes, skinned animation, SPU audio, memory card saves and world streaming.
  • pcsx-redux. Play exports the scene and boots it inside the editor, next to the scene view. Edits you make while the game runs are sent to it.

docs.title: Older docs
docs.text: The Unity-based editor (SplashEdit 2.4 and earlier) is no longer developed. Its documentation stays online at psxsplash.github.io/docs/unity, and the version menu in the header lists every older release.

docs.title: The Editor
docs.text: The window has five areas: the title bar with the menus and the run buttons, the Scene panel, the middle panel (viewport, script tabs and UI), the Inspector, and the status bar. The Project panel docks under the middle panel.

docs.title: Title bar
docs.text:
File, Edit, Object, Build, View and Help menus, then the project and scene name (a dot after it means unsaved changes), then Play, Run on hardware and Export, and undo/redo.

Menu Holds File New Project, Open, recent scenes, Save, Save As, Quit Edit Undo, Redo, Rename, Duplicate, Cut, Copy, Paste, Delete, Select None Object Add Object, Add Component, Frame Selection (F), Align with View (Ctrl+Shift+F) Build Play, Run on Hardware, Export Disc Image, and the two debug overlays View Transform tools, PS1 Look / Clean Look, Snap, Orthographic, the scene's scripts, the Project panel, and the Timeline with every cutscene and animation Help Documentation, Report a Problem

Save As keeps the scene inside the project folder, since every path in it is relative to that folder.

docs.title: Scene panel
docs.text:
The scene as a tree of objects. The header shows the object count; + adds an object and ... has more.

  • Click to select. Double-click frames the object in the viewport.
  • Drag rows to reorder or reparent. Drop a model file on a row to import it as a child.
  • Ctrl+F filters the tree by name.
  • Right-click for Rename, Duplicate, Cut, Copy, Paste, Delete, Move to Top Level, Frame in View and Pin in Inspector.

Each mesh row shows its triangle count. A warning sign means the inspector has a problem or a suggestion for that object. A crossed-out eye marks an object that starts inactive.

The tree is for organising. At export the hierarchy is flattened into world positions, so moving a parent from Lua does not move its children. See Entity.SetParent to attach objects at runtime.

docs.title: Viewport
docs.text:
The toolbar at the top left picks the transform tool: Hand (Q), Move (W), Rotate (E) and Scale (R). Next to them:

  • Snap to a 0.25 m grid. With snap off, hold Ctrl while dragging to snap.
  • Overlays: trigger boxes, interaction radii and navigation regions.

At the top right, Perspective / Orthographic and the view mode:

  • PS1 draws the scene the way the console will: 320x240, 15-bit colour with dithering, affine texture mapping, the exported vertex lighting and fog. The caption at the bottom left says so.
  • Clean draws it plainly, for placing things.

The axis widget at the top right shows the camera's orientation.

Input Does Left click Select (with Hand, left drag pans) Right drag Look around; hold W A S D Q E to fly, wheel sets the fly speed Middle drag Pan Wheel Move in and out Alt + left drag Orbit Alt + right drag Zoom F Frame the selection; Shift+F keeps following it Ctrl+Shift+F Move the selection to the camera (Align with View)

docs.title: Middle panel tabs
docs.text:
• Scene: the viewport.
  • UI: the scene's UI canvases at PS1 resolution. See UI Canvases.
  • One tab per open script: .lua files open in the Lua editor, .blocks files in the block editor.

docs.title: Inspector
docs.text:
The selected object's name, its Start active switch, then one section per component. Most sections have a switch to turn the component off, and a ... menu with Remove component. Add component at the bottom adds another. See Objects & Components.

The lock at the top right pins the inspector to the current object, so you can select others (for example to drag them into a field) while it stays put.

With nothing selected (Edit > Select None, or click empty space in the viewport), the inspector shows the scene settings.

Inspector cards flag problems and offer a one-click fix: a texture that could be 4 bpp, a mesh with no vertex colours, a player with no ground to walk on.

docs.title: Project panel
docs.text:
The project folder: a folder tree on the left, the files on the right as a grid with thumbnails or as a list. Search and the type filter (Models, Meshes, Textures, Scripts, Audio, Animations, Scenes, Fonts) cover the whole tree.

  • Drag a file onto the viewport, a scene tree row or an inspector field to use it.
  • Double-click: a scene opens, a script opens in its editor, a model or mesh is placed in the scene, anything else opens in your system's default app.
  • Right-click for Rename (F2), Delete, Reveal in file manager, and Reimport on a model.

Renaming or moving a file updates every scene in the project that uses it. Deleting is refused while something still uses the file; deleted files go to a hidden .trash/ folder in the project and are emptied after 30 days, and Ctrl+Z brings them back.

View > Project shows or hides the panel. The Timeline opens as a second tab in the same dock.

docs.title: Status bar
docs.text:
Live budgets for the scene as it would export right now:

Meter Budget VRAM 1024 KB: framebuffers, textures, CLUTs and font SPU RAM 512 KB: audio clips RAM Main RAM left for the scene after the engine: scene data, render buffers, per-object costs Triangles Triangles in the scene

The editor exports the scene in the background a moment after each edit and updates the meters. On the right: No problems or the number of export errors and warnings (click to list them), and whether everything is saved.

See Memory & Performance for what fills each budget.

docs.title: Agents (NPCs)
docs.text:
An agent is an object the engine walks along the nav regions on its own: it patrols waypoints, sees and hears the player, and runs Lua events when that changes. Guards, wandering villagers and anything that chases the player are agents.

Select an object (usually one with a mesh) and choose Add component > Agent (NPC). An agent object is always exported as a game object, even without a mesh, so Lua can reach it.

Agents need a nav bake

The engine only runs agents in a scene with nav regions: give the scene a Player or Navigation component and a floor with a Static collider (see Player, Navigation & Rooms). Without regions the agent stands still and senses nothing, and the inspector and the build's problems list say so.

docs.title: The component
docs.text:
Field Meaning Start enabled On, the agent runs from the moment the scene loads. Off, it waits for Agent.SetEnabled(self, true). Move speed Walking speed in metres per second (stored per frame at 30 fps). Default 2. Stop distance How close to a waypoint or target counts as arrived, in metres. Default 0.5. Vision Whether it sees at all. Vision range How far it sees, in metres. Default 8. 0 sees nothing. Field of view The whole cone in degrees, centred on the way the object faces (its local +Z). 360 sees all around. Default 90. Region hops How many nav regions away the target may be and still be seen: 0 is the agent's own region, at most 8. Default 2. Hearing range How far it hears, in metres. 0 (the default) hears nothing. Alert timeout Frames after it last sensed the target before onTargetLost runs. Default 90. Waypoints Patrol points in world metres, walked in order and back to the first. At object adds one where the object stands, At view centre one under the centre of the viewport. The arrows reorder them; the bin deletes one. The engine keeps 8. Idle ... Custom With a Skinned animation component on the same object: the clip the agent plays when it enters each state. Without one the section says so. Export What the agent adds to the scene file: 28 bytes plus 12 per waypoint.

The engine measures ranges as the larger of the X and Z distances, so a range is a square around the agent, not a circle. With the agent selected the viewport draws the vision cone cut by that square in pink, the hearing square in blue, and the numbered waypoints joined in patrol order. Drag a waypoint's dot to move it across the ground at its own height. The overlay toggle in the viewport toolbar hides them.

The inspector (and the build's problems list) warns about more than 8 waypoints (the rest are left out), a field of view outside 1 to 360 degrees, a state clip on an object without a skin or past its clip list, and a scene with no nav regions.

docs.title: States
docs.text:
An agent is always in one of eight states. Agent.GetState returns the number, Agent.SetState changes it.

# State What the engine does in it 0 Idle Switches to Patrol when patrolling is on and there are waypoints. 1 Patrol Walks to the current waypoint, then the next (onPatrolPoint at each). 2 Seek Follows its target actor. 3 Flee Moves away from its target actor. 4 Attack Nothing: Lua drives it. 5 Wander Walks to random spots around its nav region. 6 Investigate Walks to where it last saw or heard the target. 7 Custom Nothing: Lua drives it.

Seeing the player does not change the state by itself: switch states from the events below, for example Seek in onTargetSeen and Investigate in onTargetLost.

docs.title: Lua
docs.text:
The Agent.* functions take an actor handle: self in the agent's own script, or Actor.Find("Guard") anywhere. Positions are in engine units, Y down, like Actor.GetPosition: the scene's metres divided by its GTE scaling (100 by default), so a waypoint at (-4, 0, -4.5) m reads back as -0.040, 0, -0.045. See the Agent API.

-- On the Guard's own script.
function onTargetSeen(self, target)
    Agent.SetState(self, 2)            -- Seek
    Agent.SetTarget(self, Actor.GetPlayer())
end

function onTargetLost(self, target)
    Agent.SetState(self, 6)            -- Investigate the last known position
end

function onTargetReached(self)
    Agent.SetState(self, 1)            -- back to the patrol
end

function onPatrolPoint(self, index)
    Debug.Log("reached waypoint " .. index)
end

The agent events are object callbacks on the agent's own script (see Events): onStateEnter(self, newState, oldState), onStateExit(self, state), onTargetSeen(self, target), onTargetLost(self, target) (target is nil when it is the player), onTargetReached(self) (arrived at a position in Seek, Wander or Investigate; not while following an actor), onPatrolPoint(self, index) (0-based) and onPathBlocked(self). The engine registers onPathBlocked but never calls it yet.

docs.title: Audio
docs.text: Sound effects and music are audio clips: WAV files the editor converts to the PS1's SPU format, SPU-ADPCM, at export. All clips share the SPU's 512 KB of sound RAM; the SPU RAM meter in the status bar shows how much a scene uses.

docs.title: Adding a clip
docs.text:
Add Object > Audio clip, or Add component > Audio clip on any object, then pick a WAV file.

Field Meaning Clip A WAV file. Channels are averaged to mono. Source The WAV as it is, and the sound RAM the exported clip takes. Name What scripts play it by. Starts as the object's name. Sample rate The clip is resampled to this at export. Lower takes less sound RAM and sounds duller. 22050 is a good middle. Loop Plays again from the start when it ends, until stopped. Trim silence Cuts the quiet part at the start, so the sound starts the moment it is triggered.

docs.title: Playing a clip
docs.text:
Audio.Play("creak")                 -- volume 100, centre
Audio.Play("creak", 128, 0)         -- loudest, hard left
local channel = Audio.Play("music", 90)
Audio.Stop(channel)

Audio.Play returns the channel (0 to 23), or -1 if all 24 voices are busy. Volume runs 0 to 128, pan 0 (left) to 127 (right), 64 centre. In the block editor, play sound takes a clip name from a list of the scene's clips. A cutscene can play clips at set frames.

See the Audio API.

docs.title: CD-DA
docs.text: Audio.PlayCDDA plays audio tracks burned on a disc. The editor's disc images hold one data track, and Play and Run on hardware load files over PCdrv, so these calls have nothing to play. A scene with world streaming on ignores them as well. Use audio clips for music.

docs.title: Keeping it small
docs.text:
• ADPCM takes about 0.57 bytes per sample, so a 5-second clip at 22050 Hz is about 63 KB and at 11025 Hz about 31 KB. Drop to 11025 Hz for effects.
  • Keep clips short; loop a short bar instead of a long track.
  • There are 24 voices. Plan for the worst case of sounds at once.

docs.title: The Block Editor
docs.text:
Blocks are a second way to write the same scripts. You snap blocks into stacks, and the editor writes the Lua for the console when the scene exports. Blocks and Lua are equals: use either, or mix them, even on one object. Blocks suit logic that is a chain of events and actions. Lua suits anything with tables, loops over data or the parts of the API blocks do not cover.

A blocks file is scripts/<name>.blocks, JSON text that diffs well in git. It goes anywhere a .lua file goes: an object's Script, a Trigger box script, or the scene script.

docs.title: Making and opening a block script
docs.text:
• On a Script component, New blocks writes scripts/<object name>.blocks with a when created stack and opens it. Edit script reopens it later.
  • Double-click a .blocks file in the Project panel.
  • The scene script has the same buttons in the scene settings; its starting stack is when the scene starts.

docs.title: The editor
docs.text:
Left to right:

  • Palette. Category chips at the top (Events, Control, Objects, Sound and scenes, Variables, Operators, Input, Debug) and the blocks of the chosen category below. Hover a block to read what it does.
  • Canvas. Drag blocks out of the palette and drop them here.
  • Variables and Lua, on the right. The Lua panel shows the generated code as you build, with its line count, and lists anything that keeps it from running.

The status line says Makes Lua for the PS1. Ctrl+S saves, Ctrl+Z and Ctrl+Y undo and redo. Drag a block back to the palette (the canvas shows Drop to delete) or press Delete to remove it.

docs.title: Stacks, hats and inputs
docs.text:
A stack is a column of blocks. It starts with a hat block from Events; nothing runs until a stack starts with one. Statements snap under it, and a stack without a hat is loose and makes no code. Two stacks with the same hat are merged into one function, in the order they sit.

Rounded and pointed blocks (Operators, Variables, positions) are values. Drop them into the slots of other blocks: if takes a pointed true/false block, move ... by takes three numbers. Click a field in a block to type or pick a value: an object (self or any object in the scene), a controller button, a sound clip or a cutscene.

docs.title: Blocks
docs.text:
Category Blocks Events when created, every frame, when the player touches me, when the player interacts, when button is pressed, when button is released, when enabled, when disabled, when the scene starts, when the player enters the trigger, when the player leaves the trigger Control wait n seconds, if, if/else, repeat, while, repeat until, wait until, stop this script Objects show, hide, move by, move to, x/y/z position of Sound and scenes play sound, play cutscene, load scene Variables set, change by, and a block for each variable Operators numbers, text, true/false, + - * /, mod, pick random, join, = < >, and, or, not Input button held? Debug log, frame count

The event hats are the same events as in Lua: when created is onCreate, when the player interacts is onInteract, and so on. See Event Callbacks. wait blocks pause the stack and let the rest of the game run.

docs.title: Variables
docs.text:
Make a variable in the Variables panel, type its name and pick its kind: Number, True-false or Text. A variable belongs to this script. Names take letters, digits and _ and cannot start with a digit; names that would clash with Lua keywords, the API tables or the event function names are refused.

Numbers with decimals are fine in blocks. The generated Lua writes 0.5 as a fixed-point value for you; see Fixed-Point Math.

docs.title: Convert to Lua
docs.text: Right-click the script's tab and pick Convert to Lua... to turn a blocks file into a Lua file. Every reference to the script follows. It is one way: the editor cannot turn Lua back into blocks, though Ctrl+Z undoes the conversion. Do it when a script outgrows blocks.

docs.title: What blocks do not cover
docs.text: Blocks cover the events and actions in the table above. Everything else in the API, tables, and your own functions are Lua. Block scripts and Lua scripts in one scene work side by side.

docs.title: Building & Running
docs.text:
There is no separate build step. The editor exports your scene in the background a moment after each edit, so the status bar is always showing the real budgets for what would ship: VRAM, SPU RAM, main RAM and triangles. Play, Run on hardware and Export use that same export.

You want Press Where it runs To try the scene now Play (F5) pcsx-redux inside the editor To test on a console Run on hardware (Ctrl+F5) A PS1 with Unirom, over a serial cable To hand it to someone Export (Ctrl+B) A .bin + .cue disc image

The details are in Play, Hardware and Discs.

docs.title: What an export writes
docs.text:
For each scene in the build list, the editor writes files named scene_<i>:

File Holds .splashpack Objects, meshes, collision, navigation, UI, cutscenes, animations and the Lua scripts, compiled .vram Textures and palettes, packed into VRAM .spu Audio clips, as SPU-ADPCM .geo Streamed level geometry, when streaming is on .loading The loading screen, when there is one

Block scripts are turned into Lua at this point. Lua is checked by the same compiler as the Lua editor uses.

docs.title: Problems
docs.text:
The right of the status bar reads No problems, or the number of errors and warnings. Click it for the list.

  • Errors stop the export. Play and Export tell you what to fix: a missing file, a track that targets an object that is not there, a portal with no Room, a script that does not compile.
  • Warnings do not stop anything. They flag things like a texture that could be 4 bpp, a model with no vertex colours or a long skinned clip.

docs.title: Budgets
docs.text:
The meters are the console's limits:

Meter Limit VRAM 1024 KB SPU RAM 512 KB RAM What main RAM leaves for the scene after the engine

When one turns red, see Memory & Performance.

docs.title: Debug overlays
docs.text: Build > Performance Overlay and Build > Room Debug Overlay boot a psxsplash build that draws an FPS counter and heap bar, or the room wireframe. See Debug overlays.

docs.title: Models
docs.text:
The editor reads glTF (.gltf, .glb), FBX and OBJ (with its .mtl) directly, and .blend through Blender (see Installation).

To bring a model in, drop the file on the viewport, on a row in the Scene tree (it becomes a child of that row), or into the Project panel. Choosing a model in a Mesh component's Model field works too. The editor copies the file into the project's models/ folder, if it is not already there, and writes:

File What it is models/<name>.mesh The whole model baked into one mesh, one submesh per material models/<name>/<node>.mesh One mesh per node of the model, for placing the parts as separate objects models/<name>_<n>.png The base colour textures its materials use models/<name>/<clip>.anim One file per animation in the file, for skinned models models/<name>.<ext>.import.json The import settings, beside the source file

Textures larger than 256 texels on a side are scaled down to fit a PS1 texture page. A texture the importer cannot find is a warning, not an error.

docs.title: Import settings
docs.text:
Select a model file in the Project panel and the inspector shows its Import settings. Each change re-imports the model and every copy placed in the scene.

Setting Effect Scale Multiplies the model's size. 1 keeps the size in the file, in metres. Up axis From file believes the file. Y up or Z up overrides it, for a model that comes in lying on its back. Normals Import keeps the file's normals (flat shading where it has none). Recompute works them out from the faces. Smoothing angle With Recompute: faces meeting at less than this angle are shaded smooth across the edge. Merge meshes On: each placed copy is one object drawing a single mesh. Off: the file's parts become child objects. Bit depth for new objects The texture bit depth of objects made from this model from now on. Lighting for new objects Whether runtime lights light these objects; see Lighting.

Merging objects also cuts the RAM each object costs at load. A scene with over a thousand objects can run out of RAM on object count alone, and the scene settings then offer to select the biggest group. Merge meshes is the fix.

Every warning from the last import is listed under the settings with a suggested fix.

docs.title: Textures
docs.text:
Textures are PNG files. Assign one in a Mesh component's Texture field (one per material) by clicking the field and picking a file, or by dragging it from the Project panel. The editor converts it to PS1 colours on export.

Under the texture field, a preview shows the Source next to the PS1 result, with the bit depth, palette size, colour count and an error figure. If the PS1 version looks wrong, this is where you see why before you press Play.

See Materials & Bit Depth for what 4, 8 and 16 bpp cost.

docs.title: Lighting
docs.text: The PS1 has no per-pixel lighting. psxsplash lights a mesh in one of two ways: colours baked into its vertices at export, or a few runtime point lights added per triangle on the console.

docs.title: The Light component
docs.text:
Add one from Add Object > Point light, or Add component > Light on any object.

Field Meaning Type Point shines in every direction, Spot in a cone, Directional from far away (like the sun). Colour The light's colour. Intensity How bright it is. 1 is normal. Range How far it reaches before fading out. Point and spot only. Spot angle, Inner angle Spot only. Inside the inner cone the light is at full strength and fades out to the spot angle. 0 fades from 80% of the spot angle.

The switch on the component header turns it off. The viewport's PS1 view shows the baked result on the walls and floor, so you see a light's effect as you move it.

docs.title: Baked lighting
docs.text:
A mesh with Lighting: Baked vertex (the default) gets the scene's lights baked into its vertex colours when the scene exports. It costs nothing at runtime, and it is what the courtyard example uses. Triangles are lit per vertex, so large triangles shade smoothly only if the mesh has vertices to carry it: split big floors and walls if a light looks blotchy.

Smooth normals on the mesh changes whether the bake treats surfaces as flat or curved. See Materials & Bit Depth.

docs.title: Runtime lights
docs.text:
A point light can instead run on the console, so scripts can move it, recolour it and switch it on and off with the Light API, and timeline tracks can animate it. In the scene file this is "runtime": true on the light component (see the scene format notes in the editor's repository); the inspector does not show a switch for it yet.

  • At most 16 runtime lights per scene.
  • At most 4 reach one mesh. Extra lights are left out.
  • Skinned meshes are not lit at runtime.
  • A mesh lit at runtime leaves runtime lights out of its baked colours; every other mesh bakes them in.

docs.title: Dynamic lighting
docs.text:
Which meshes runtime lights affect is set per mesh and starts from the model's import settings, Lighting for new objects:

Setting Behaviour Auto Lit if a runtime light's range reaches the mesh at export. On Always lit. Use it for meshes that move into a light's range. Smooth Lit per vertex. Smoother on big triangles, at about nine times the cost. Off Never lit at runtime.

Every lit triangle costs CPU time. Keep ranges small, and leave lights that never move baked.

docs.title: The Lua Editor
docs.text:
Lua files open in a tab next to Scene and UI. Open one by double-clicking it in the Project panel, or with Edit script on a Script component. New Lua on a Script component writes scripts/<object name>.lua with onCreate ready to fill in and opens it. See Lua scripting for the language and the API.

You can write every script in Lua, build every script from blocks, or mix them in one scene. Neither is the default, and both end up as the same Lua on the console.

docs.title: What the editor does for you
docs.text:
• Highlighting for Lua 5.2 and the psxsplash API.
  • Compile check. A moment after you stop typing, the script is compiled the way the exporter will compile it. The bar at the bottom reads Compiles for the PS1, or shows the first error with its line; click it to jump there, and a squiggle marks the spot.
  • Autocomplete. Type Entity. and the list shows every function in the table, with its signature. Ctrl+Space opens the list on demand. Enter or Tab accepts. Your own functions and variables are listed too.
  • Signature hints while you type the arguments of a call.
  • Go to definition. Ctrl+click a name, or press F12, to jump to where your script defines it. Hovering an API function shows what it does.
  • Find and replace. Ctrl+F finds, Ctrl+H replaces. Options: Match case, Whole word, regular expression (with $1 in the replacement) and Preserve case, plus Find in selection. F3 and Shift+F3 step through matches; Ctrl+Alt+Enter replaces all in one undo step.
  • Ctrl+/ comments the selection. Tab and Shift+Tab indent and outdent.
  • Ctrl+S saves; Ctrl+Z and Ctrl+Y undo and redo. The status bar shows the line and column, and Lua 5.2 (psxlua).

Press Play and open scripts are saved first.

docs.title: Files changed outside the editor
docs.text:
If a script changes on disk while it is open (your own text editor, git) and the tab has unsaved edits, the tab says Changed on disk and offers Reload or Keep mine. Ctrl+Z after a reload brings your edits back. A file deleted on disk can be written again with Save.

Closing a tab with unsaved edits asks first: Save, Don't save or Cancel.

docs.title: Using VS Code or another editor
docs.text:
View > Set up external editor (VS Code) writes two files into the project folder:

  • psxsplash.d.lua, the psxsplash API as lua-language-server definitions: completion and signatures for every table and function, with hover docs where the API reference has them, made from the same list the editor's autocomplete uses.
  • .luarc.json, which sets Lua 5.2 and turns off the libraries the PS1 does not have (math, io, os, require). It is only written when the project has none, so your own settings are kept.

Open the project folder in VS Code with the Lua extension (sumneko) installed. When a newer editor opens the project, it brings psxsplash.d.lua up to date on its own.

docs.title: Fixed-point numbers
docs.text: The PS1 has no floating-point unit, so a decimal like 0.5 is not a number in these scripts. Read Fixed-Point Math first. The compile check accepts what the compiler accepts, so it will not flag a script that does the wrong arithmetic.

docs.title: Materials & Bit Depth
docs.text: A mesh has one material per submesh. Each material is a Texture (a PNG) and a Colour. With a texture, the colour is not shown in the inspector; without one, the material is that flat colour.

docs.title: Texture bit depth
docs.text:
VRAM is 1 MB and every texture lives there, so bit depth is the biggest lever you have.

Depth Colours VRAM per texel Notes 4 bpp 16 4 bits Needs a 16-entry palette (a CLUT). Smallest. 8 bpp 256 8 bits Palette of 256. The default for new meshes. 16 bpp 32768 16 bits No palette; 15-bit colour. Largest.

The depth is per mesh component. The inspector shows it next to the texture's size, for example 64 x 64 · 8 bpp. Compare under the preview flips between the source and the PS1 result.

docs.title: The 4 bpp suggestion
docs.text:
When every texture on a mesh has 16 colours or fewer, and 4 bpp would use less VRAM, the inspector shows a card:

Texture could be 4 bpp: crate.png has 7 colours and takes 4.02 KB of VRAM. At 4 bpp it keeps every colour and takes 2.02 KB.

Convert to 4 bpp applies it in one undo step. The scene tree marks the object with a warning sign until you do. The suggestion never appears for textures with more than 16 colours; those would lose colour at 4 bpp, and the PS1 preview under the texture field shows exactly how much.

To change the depth the other way, set Bit depth for new objects in the model's import settings and re-place the model.

docs.title: Mesh colours and lighting
docs.text:
Lighting on a mesh picks where its vertex colours come from:

Option Meaning Baked vertex Light from the scene's lights is baked into the vertices at export. Costs nothing at runtime. Flat One flat colour. Mesh colours The colours stored in the model file. A model with none shows flat grey (127, 127, 127), and the inspector says so with a Use baked lighting fix.

Smooth normals (Baked vertex only) bakes the lighting as if the surface were smoothly curved. Off keeps the model's own normals, for hard edges.

docs.title: Limits worth knowing
docs.text:
• Textures are at most 256 x 256; larger images are scaled down on import.
  • All of a scene's textures share VRAM with two framebuffers and the font column. The VRAM meter in the status bar shows the total; the scene settings' VRAM layout shows where each atlas sits and lets you reserve areas.
  • Several materials on one mesh each take their own texture.

See Memory & Performance.

docs.title: The player
docs.text:
One Player component per scene marks where the player starts and how it moves (fields in Objects & Components). Put the Player component where you want the player to start; the exporter drops its start point straight down onto the nearest upward-facing floor within 100 units and raises it by the player's Height.

The player walks on a navigation mesh baked from your geometry, not on physics:

  1. Give floors and ramps a Collider set to Static.
  2. The export bakes walkable regions from static colliders that are flat enough (Max slope), wide enough (Radius) and reachable by steps no taller than Step height.
  3. The player stays on those regions. Static walls stop it.

If the bake finds nothing, the inspector says The player can't walk: with no ground, the camera stays at the origin and the controller is ignored. When meshes lack a collider, Make meshes walkable gives them a Static one.

docs.title: Seeing the bake
docs.text: Select nothing, and the scene settings have a Navigation section: the number of regions and portals, and switches for Show in viewport (region outlines), Labels (R0, R1 ... click one to select it) and Portals (the edges the player can cross between regions). Region shows a selected region's floor height and surface.

docs.title: The Navigation component
docs.text:
A Navigation component bakes walkable ground without a player, or overrides the player's bake: Agent height, Agent radius, Step height, Max slope. If the scene has one, its values win.

Finer bake settings (cell size, region merging) are in the scene file and keep their defaults; see the scene format notes in the editor's repository.

docs.title: Colliders and triggers
docs.text:
Component Does Collider: Static Walkable and solid scenery. Part of the nav bake. Collider: Dynamic A box tested against the player every frame. Fires onCollideWithPlayer. Scripts can move it. Trigger box A volume that calls onTriggerEnter(index) and onTriggerExit(index) on its own script. Interactable Calls onInteract when the player presses a button within Radius.

A dynamic collider's box does not turn when you rotate the object.

docs.title: Rooms and portals
docs.text:
Indoor scenes draw faster if only the rooms the camera can see are drawn. Add Room objects as boxes around areas, and Portal objects on the openings between them.

  • Room: Size and Offset are the box in metres. Each static triangle goes to the room whose box holds most of its corners; triangles that fit none go to a catch-all room that is always drawn. The component shows what the last export made of it: triangles, cells and portals.
  • Portal: Room A and Room B pick the two rooms (by name, so keep Room names unique) and Width and Height size the opening on the object's X and Y axes. The viewport's arrow points from A into B. From either room, the camera sees into the other through the portal.

The scene settings read Culling: rooms and portals, N rooms once one Room exists; with none it reads Culling: frustum (BVH). The Scene type dropdown is stored but not read by the engine: culling follows the Rooms.

A scene holds at most 31 Rooms. A portal with a missing, duplicated or identical Room names shows what to fix under the component, and the export stops until you do.

Press Build > Room Debug Overlay and then Play to see each room's wireframe in the game.

docs.title: Objects & Components
docs.text: Everything in a scene is an object: a name, a transform, a Start active switch, and any number of components. An object with no components is an empty, useful for grouping.

docs.title: Adding objects
docs.text:
+ in the Scene panel or Object > Add Object... (Ctrl+A) opens a searchable list of starting points:

Object Starts with Empty Only a transform Mesh A Mesh component; pick its file in the inspector Point light A Light Player A Player Trigger box A Trigger box Interactable An Interactable Audio clip An Audio clip Script A Script Navigation A Navigation component Room A Room Portal A Portal Agent (NPC) An Agent

New objects appear in front of the camera, after the selected object. Dropping a model file on the viewport or the scene tree also makes an object; see Importing.

Add component at the bottom of the inspector (or Object > Add Component...) adds a component to the selected object. Each component type can be added once per object. Collider and Skinned animation need a Mesh first.

docs.title: Transform
docs.text:
Position in metres and Rotation in degrees, both relative to the parent, and Scale per axis. Drag the viewport gizmo or type values. At export, positions are divided by the scene's GTE scaling (see Scene Settings) into PS1 units, so everything has to sit within 8 x the scaling of the origin: 800 m at the default of 100.

Start active off ships the object switched off. Its meshes are not drawn until a script calls Entity.SetActive(object, true); its lights still bake.

docs.title: Mesh
docs.text: Draws a model. Model is the .mesh file (or pick a .glb, .gltf, .fbx, .obj or .blend to import one); then one Texture and colour per material, Lighting and Smooth normals. See Materials & Bit Depth and Lighting.

docs.title: Collider
docs.text:
Shape Effect Static Solid scenery. Feeds the navigation bake: the player walks on static floors and is stopped by static walls. Dynamic Can be moved by scripts. Tested against the player every frame, and the only kind that fires onCollideWithPlayer. None No collision.

Rotating a dynamic collider

Its box does not rotate with the object. See Known Issues.

docs.title: Script
docs.text: Runs a script for this object. File points at a .lua or .blocks file; New blocks and New Lua create one in scripts/ named after the object, and Edit script opens it. Each object gets its own copy of the script's state. See Lua scripting and The Block Editor.

docs.title: Light
docs.text: Lights the meshes around it. See Lighting.

docs.title: Player
docs.text:
Where the player starts and how it moves. One per scene.

Field Meaning Height Eye height Radius How wide the player is, for walls and the nav bake Move speed Walking speed Sprint speed Speed while the sprint button is held Jump height How high a jump goes Gravity How fast the player falls; about 9.8 is Earth Step height, Max slope What the nav bake treats as walkable Cell size, Cell height The nav bake's voxel size

See Player, Navigation & Rooms.

docs.title: Navigation
docs.text: Bakes walkable ground without a player, or overrides the player's bake settings: Agent height, Agent radius, Step height, Max slope, Cell size, Cell height.

docs.title: Trigger box
docs.text: An axis-aligned box (Size, in metres, centred on the object) that calls a script when the player walks in or out. Script is the trigger's own script, separate from the object's Script component; it gets onTriggerEnter and onTriggerExit. New blocks and New Lua make a <name>_trigger file.

docs.title: Interactable
docs.text:
Calls the object's script (onInteract) when the player presses a button nearby.

Field Meaning Radius How close the player has to be Button The pad button that uses it (Cross by default) Repeatable On: usable again after Cooldown. Off: works once. Show prompt, Prompt Shows a UI canvas while the player is in range. The canvas name must fit in 15 characters. Require facing, Facing angle The player has to look toward the object

docs.title: Audio clip
docs.text: A sound scripts can play by name. See Audio.

docs.title: Skinned animation
docs.text: Plays animation clips on a skinned mesh. See Skinned Animation.

docs.title: Agent (NPC)
docs.text: A character the engine walks along the nav regions: patrol waypoints, vision and hearing, and a skin clip per state. See Agents.

docs.title: Room and Portal
docs.text: Room boxes and the openings between them, for culling indoor scenes. See Player, Navigation & Rooms.

docs.title: Copy, paste and duplicate
docs.text: Duplicate (Ctrl+D), Cut, Copy and Paste work on the selected object and its children. Paste puts the copy after the selection. Names stay unique: a second "Crate" becomes "Crate (2)".

docs.title: Names matter
docs.text: Scripts, timeline tracks, portals and interact prompts find objects by name. Rename with F2 or by double-clicking the name in the inspector. Keep names unique among objects a script looks up.

docs.title: Scene Settings
docs.text: Select nothing (Edit > Select None, or click empty space in the viewport) and the inspector shows the scene's settings, one section after another.

docs.title: Scene script
docs.text: File is a script, blocks or Lua, that runs for the whole scene, with New blocks, New Lua and Edit script like any Script component. A Lua scene script gets onSceneCreationStart and onSceneCreationEnd; a block one starts with when the scene starts. See Event Callbacks.

docs.title: Cutscenes and animations
docs.text: Every cutscene and animation in the scene, each with Edit in timeline. See Cutscenes & Animations.

docs.title: Rendering
docs.text:
Field Meaning Background The colour the screen clears to every frame. With fog on, distant triangles fade to it. Fog Fades distant triangles to the background colour, and culls anything wholly past the fog wall. Density Fog density, 1 to 10. Kept while fog is off. GTE scaling Editor units per PS1 unit, default 100. Positions export as value divided by this, in 16-bit fixed point, so everything must sit within 8 x the scaling of the origin: 800 m at 100. Smaller is finer, larger reaches farther. Scene type Exterior or Interior. Stored in the scene, but the engine does not read it: culling follows Room objects.

A caption underneath says which culling the scene will use.

docs.title: Loading screen
docs.text:
Canvas picks a UI canvas of this scene that psxsplash draws while the scene loads. The canvas is left out of the scene itself.

The progress bar must be named loading

The engine fills only a progress bar whose Name is exactly loading, from 0 to 100 as the scene loads. A bar with any other name stays at its initial value, and the settings warn you. The loading screen is drawn directly while the scene loads, so animation tracks and UI.SetProgress do not run on it. Line elements are not drawn on it either.

docs.title: Build scenes
docs.text: The scenes that Play and Export write, in order. Add scene picks from the .scene files in the project; the arrows reorder and the x takes one out. Play and Export start at scene 0, and Scene.Load(i) opens scene i of this list. With an empty list, the open scene is written alone.

docs.title: VRAM layout
docs.text: A map of the 1024 x 512 VRAM: the two framebuffers, the font column (x 960) and the texture atlases. Prohibited areas are rectangles you drag out for textures and palettes to stay out of, for example to keep room for something your game draws itself. Without any, the packer may use all of VRAM except the framebuffers and x 960.

docs.title: Disc
docs.text: Volume label and Licence for exported disc images. See Play, Hardware and Discs.

docs.title: Render buffers
docs.text:
Two sizes the console allocates for drawing. Both start at auto, sized from the scene; type a number to override, and the undo arrow goes back to auto.

Buffer Meaning Ordering table Depth slots the renderer sorts triangles into, back to front. One slot per depth step, so this is also how far the camera sees: anything wholly beyond it is not drawn. 8 bytes of RAM per slot. Primitive buffer Bytes of GPU commands one frame can build: every triangle drawn, plus sprites and text. If a frame needs more, the game stops with "Out of memory". It costs twice its size in RAM, once per frame being drawn.

While the game runs under Play, the settings add the peaks it actually reached: the farthest depth drawn and the busiest frame's bytes. The section warns when the scene may cut off or run out.

docs.title: BVH
docs.text: The bounding volume hierarchy psxsplash culls with: it draws only the triangles in boxes the camera can see. The section reports the node, leaf and triangle-reference counts. Show in viewport draws the boxes over the scene, one colour per level, and Depth sets the deepest level drawn (0 is the root box around the whole scene).

docs.title: Navigation
docs.text: The nav bake's region and portal counts, with the viewport overlays. See Player, Navigation & Rooms.

docs.title: World streaming
docs.text: See World Streaming.

docs.title: Memory card
docs.text:
For MemCard.Save and friends. Enable saves packs the settings into this scene; off, the console keeps the last scene's settings, so give every scene of a game the same values.

Field Meaning Region BA America, BE Europe, BI Japan. Starts every save filename. Product code For example SLUS-00000, up to 10 characters. Save title What the BIOS memory card screen shows, ASCII only, at most 32 characters. ", ', -, \ and ~ show as ?. MemCard.Save's fourth argument overrides it per save. Icon One to three 16 x 16 images. Two or three animate.

A save's filename is region + product code + the key you pass to MemCard.Save, cut at 20 characters. With a 10-character product code only the first 8 characters of a key count; the settings warn when region and product fill all 20 and every key would save to the same file. A save made under one product code is not found under another.

docs.title: Skinned Animation
docs.text: A skinned mesh is a model with a skeleton. The PS1 skins it rigidly: each vertex follows the one joint that influences it most, and the engine draws at most 64 joints per model.

docs.title: Getting one in
docs.text:
Import a glTF or FBX with a skin (see Importing). The editor keeps the skeleton in the .mesh and writes one models/<name>/<clip>.anim file per animation in the model file. Each clip's name is what Lua plays it by, 1 to 24 characters and unique per object. FBX animations are baked at 30 Hz.

Place the model, then Add component > Skinned animation (it needs a Mesh with a skeleton first).

docs.title: The component
docs.text:
Field Meaning Clips The .anim files this object can play, at most 16. Click to pick them; the pick replaces the list. Bake rate Frames per second the clips are sampled at, 1 to 30. Default 15. The engine blends between frames, so a low rate still looks smooth. Baked What the export makes of the clips at this bake rate: the bones and triangles, then each clip's frame count and size in KB, and the skin data total.

A Long clip card appears when a clip bakes to more than 1000 frames; lower the bake rate or trim the clip. A looping clip stores its frames over [0, length) and wraps from the last frame to the first, so the end pose is not stored twice.

docs.title: Playing clips
docs.text:
SkinnedAnim.Play("Hero", "walk", { loop = true })
SkinnedAnim.Play("Hero", "attack", {
    onComplete = function()
        SkinnedAnim.Play("Hero", "idle", { loop = true })
    end
})

The first argument is the object name, the second the clip name. A cutscene or animation can start a clip at a frame with a Skin clip event. SkinnedAnim.GetBone returns where a bone is, to attach things to it. See the SkinnedAnim API.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Skinned meshes are not lit by runtime lights.
  • Bones cost RAM per frame of each clip. Fewer bones, shorter clips and a lower bake rate all shrink the scene. See Memory & Performance.

docs.title: Sprite Sheets
docs.text:
A sprite sheet is a texture cut into a grid of equal cells, plus named animations: runs of cells the engine plays one after another. Lua makes sprites from a sheet and plays its animations by name. Use them for 2D characters, effects, pickups and anything else drawn as a flat picture over the scene.

Sheets belong to the scene, not to an object. With nothing selected (Edit > Select None, or click empty space in the viewport) the inspector shows the scene settings; the Sprite sheets section is among them.

docs.title: Sheets
docs.text:
Add sheet opens a list of the project's images. Pick one and the editor adds a sheet named after the file (with a number in brackets if that name is taken), with 16 x 16 cells, 4 bpp and one animation called idle. The list above it shows each sheet with its grid and animation count; click one to edit it, the bin deletes it with its animations. When the texture does not divide into cells the row shows only the animation count, in orange.

Field Meaning Name What Lua finds the sheet by: Sprite.Create("hero"). At most 24 characters, unique in the scene. Texture The image cut into cells. Cells are numbered row by row from 0 at the top left. Bit depth 4 bpp, 16 colours, 8 bpp, 256 colours or 16 bpp, direct colour. 4 bpp takes a quarter of the VRAM of 16 bpp. Cell Width (W) and height (H) of one cell in pixels, 1 to 255. The line under it shows the grid, for example "2 x 2 cells, 64 x 32 px", or says the texture is not a whole number of cells.

docs.title: Animations
docs.text:
Each sheet has its own list of animations. Add animation adds one called anim (numbered if taken) that starts on the cell after the sheet's last animation ends (or on cell 0 when that is past the end of the sheet). Click an animation to edit it; the bin deletes it. The row shows its cells, its frame time and whether it loops.

Field Meaning Name What Lua plays it by: Sprite.PlayAnim(sprite, "walk"). At most 24 characters, and unique across all sheets in the scene (see below). First cell The cell it starts on, counted row by row from 0 at the top left. Frames How many cells it plays, one after another, 1 to 255. Frame time How long each cell shows, in vsyncs, 1 to 255. The line under it gives the time in milliseconds. Loop On: back to the first cell after the last. Off: it stops on the last cell.

The engine counts vsyncs at 60 a second from real time, whatever frame rate the scene runs at: a frame time of 6 is 100 ms a cell, a frame time of 2 is 33 ms.

The preview at the bottom shows the whole sheet with its grid and the selected animation's cells outlined, and next to it the cell the engine would show now, played at the engine's timing. It uses the converted texture, so it shows the PS1 colours at the sheet's bit depth. Every change in the section is one undo step.

docs.title: Transparency
docs.text: Sheet textures are converted with cutout on: a texel with alpha below half is transparent, everything else is opaque. There is no partial transparency. At 4 bpp and 8 bpp one palette entry is spent on transparency, so a 4 bpp sheet keeps 15 colours for the picture and an 8 bpp one 255.

docs.title: Limits and build errors
docs.text:
The section lists what the build would refuse as you type, and the build stops on the same errors. The last one is only found when the build packs VRAM:

  • more than 16 sheets or more than 64 animations in the scene (all sheets together);
  • a sheet with no name, or two sheets with the same name;
  • a sheet with no texture, or a texture that cannot be loaded;
  • a cell side outside 1 to 255 pixels;
  • a texture that is not a whole number of cells ("the texture is 64x40, not a whole number of 16x16 cells");
  • more than 255 cells in a sheet: use bigger cells;
  • an animation with no name, or two animations with the same name, even on different sheets;
  • an animation with fewer than 1 frame, or a frame time outside 1 to 255 vsyncs;
  • an animation whose cells run past the end of its sheet;
  • a sheet whose texture, once packed into VRAM, would run past its 256 x 256 texture page: use a smaller image or a lower bit depth.

A name longer than 24 characters is a warning, not an error: it is stored cut to 24, and Lua must use the cut name.

Animation names must be unique across the scene because Sprite.AnimIndex and Sprite.PlayAnim search every sheet and take the first animation with that name. Name them after the sheet: hero_idle, hero_walk, bat_fly.

docs.title: Sprites come from Lua
docs.text:
Sheets only describe pictures. There is nothing to place in the scene: a script creates each sprite at run time with Sprite.Create, moves it and plays its animations. The engine has a pool of 128 sprites.

local hero

function onCreate(self)
    hero = Sprite.Create("hero")          -- the sheet's name; -1 if missing or the pool is full
    Sprite.SetPos(hero, 152, 104)         -- screen pixels, top left corner
    Sprite.PlayAnim(hero, "hero_idle")
end

docs.title: Facing directions
docs.text:
For a character drawn from several directions, click Add direction set under the sheet's animations. Give it a name, 4 or 8 directions, the frames each direction plays and the cell the first one starts on: it adds one animation per direction (walk_n, walk_ne, walk_e ... walk_nw), each starting where the previous one ends, so a sheet with one row per direction fills in by itself.

n is the character seen from behind, facing the same way as the camera, and the names go round clockwise: e faces +X, s faces the camera. Select any animation of the set to see the dial and the line to call each frame:

Sprite.PlayAnim(hero, "walk_n")           -- start the cycle once
-- every frame:
local yaw = Entity.GetRotationY(self) - Camera.GetRotation().y   -- 1 = 180 degrees
Sprite.SetFacingFromYaw(hero, "walk_n", 8, yaw)

SetFacingFromYaw plays the animation of the direction nearest to the yaw without restarting the walk cycle, and keeps whether it is playing: start it with PlayAnim first, or the sprite holds still on the new direction's cell. The set's animations must stay together and in order in the list; Problems warns when one is missing or out of place.

docs.title: What is drawn
docs.text:
Sprites are drawn in front of all 3D geometry and behind UI canvases, in layers 0 (front) to 11 (Sprite.SetLayer).

  • Screen plane (the default): the position is in screen pixels, shifted by the view offset (Sprite.SetViewOffset). This is what the engine draws.
  • World plane (Sprite.BindToActor(sprite, actor, 1), or Sprite.SetWorldPos): carried by the engine but not drawn yet. A sprite on the world plane is invisible.

Every function, with its arguments and ranges, is in the Sprite API.

docs.title: HUD sprites
docs.text: A UI canvas Image can show one cell of a sprite sheet instead of its own texture: pick the sheet in the Image's Sheet field and click a cell. It draws on the canvas like any element, and Lua switches cells with UI.SetFrame. The sheet is packed once, whether Lua sprites, Images or both use it.

docs.title: Tilemaps
docs.text:
A tilemap is a grid of tiles drawn from the cells of one sprite sheet, the sheet's cell size being the tile size. The engine draws it as a 2D floor behind every sprite, and Lua asks it two things: which pixels can be walked on, and where its tagged objects are (a spawn point, a pickup, a switch). A scene has at most one tilemap.

Each cell of the map holds a brush. A brush says which tileset cell to draw, whether the cell is walkable, and whether it is an object. You set up the brushes in the scene inspector and paint with them in the Tilemap tab.

docs.title: The Tilemap section
docs.text:
The map belongs to the scene. With nothing selected (Edit > Select None, or click empty space in the viewport) the inspector shows the scene settings; the Tilemap section is among them, under Sprite sheets.

Add tilemap makes a 20 x 15 map (a 320 x 240 screen of 16 px tiles), all empty, drawn from the scene's first sprite sheet, with two brushes: floor on cell 0, walkable, and wall on cell 1, solid. Until the scene has a sprite sheet the button does nothing and the section says "Add a sprite sheet first: the tiles are drawn from its cells." Paint opens the Tilemap tab; Remove deletes the map with its brushes and cells (Ctrl+Z brings it back).

Field Meaning Tileset The sprite sheet the tiles are drawn from. Its cell size is the tile size. Renaming the sheet keeps it picked. Size Width (W) and height (H) in tiles, 1 to 256 each. A smaller size cuts the map at the right and bottom; the cells both sizes share are kept.

Under the size, two lines give the tile size and the map in pixels ("16 x 16 px tiles, 320 x 240 px"), then the object count and what the map adds to the splashpack ("2 objects, 632 bytes in the splashpack": 20 bytes, plus 2 a cell, plus 6 an object).

Every change in the section is one undo step.

docs.title: Brushes
docs.text:
The Brushes list shows each brush with its tile, its cell number, walkable or solid, and its kind when it has one. Click one to edit it; the bin deletes it, and the cells painted with it become empty. Add brush adds one called brush (numbered if taken) that draws the cell after the last brush's (back to cell 0 past the end of the sheet).

Field Meaning Name Shown in the palette; only for you. Up to 32 characters. Tile The tileset cell it draws, row by row from 0 at the top left. Click the thumbnail to pick the cell from the tileset, or type the number. -1, or Hole (draws nothing) in the picker, draws nothing (a hole). Walkable On: a player can stand here. Off: a wall; Tile.MoveActor stops at it. Object kind 0, (none): a plain tile. Anything else makes each cell painted with it an object Lua finds with Tile.ObjectCount and Tile.ObjectAt. The game decides what a kind means. Object id Only for a brush with a kind. The id Tile.ObjectAt gives each of its cells, 0 to 255; -1 (auto) numbers them 1, 2, 3 in reading order, per kind.

An empty cell, and a cell whose brush is a hole, draws nothing and is solid, whatever the brush's Walkable says. A hole brush makes no objects either.

docs.title: Kinds and ids
docs.text:
The engine never interprets a kind or an id: they are two numbers, 0 to 255, that it stores and hands back. Pick a number for each kind of thing your game places on the map (1 for spawn points, 2 for coins, say) and give the brush that kind.

At export, every cell painted with a brush that has a kind becomes one object, in reading order: rows from the top, each row left to right. A brush with an Object id of -1 numbers its cells per kind as they come in that order, 1, 2, 3, counting every auto-numbered cell of that kind whatever brush painted it. A brush with a fixed id gives all its cells that id, and does not move the count, so mixing fixed and auto ids in one kind can give two objects the same id.

Kind names are labels for the kind numbers, shown in the Object kind list and the palette. They are for you only; the engine and Lua see the numbers. Name a kind adds a label for the next number ("kind 1", "kind 2"), and the bin on the last one removes it.

docs.title: The Tilemap tab
docs.text:
While the scene has a tilemap, a Tilemap tab sits beside the Scene and UI tabs. It shows the map with the tileset in its PS1 colours, on a checkerboard where nothing is drawn, with faint grid lines on the tile edges. Cells painted with a brush that no longer exists, or whose cell is past the end of the sheet, show red. Object cells have a small square of their brush's colour in the top left corner.

The palette on the left lists the Eraser and every brush with its tile, walkable or solid, and its kind and id. Click one to paint with it.

Control Does Left button Paints the selected brush. Dragging paints every cell along the way. Right button Erases. Shift+drag Fills a rectangle on release, with the brush (left button) or empty (right button). Alt+click Picks the brush of the cell under the pointer (the Eraser for an empty cell). Wheel Zooms about the pointer, from 25% to 1600%. Middle drag Pans.

A stroke, from press to release, is one undo step, and so is a rectangle. The line under the map shows the cell under the pointer ("0, 3 wall, solid", or "empty") and, on the right, the map's size, tile size and zoom.

docs.title: Export
docs.text:
The section lists what export would refuse as you type, and export stops on the same errors:

  • "The tilemap has no tileset: pick the sprite sheet its tiles are drawn from"
  • "The tilemap's tileset '...' is not one of the scene's sprite sheets: pick one"
  • "Tile brush '...' draws tileset cell N, but '...' has C (0..C-1)": the brush's cell is past the end of the sheet.
  • "Tile brush '...' draws tileset cell N: use -1 for a hole": a cell below -1, only possible by editing the scene file.
  • "N tilemap cells are painted with a brush that no longer exists: repaint or erase them": also only from the scene file, since deleting a brush in the editor empties its cells.
  • "N tilemap object tiles, psxsplash holds at most 128: paint fewer cells with brushes that have a kind"

The tileset is a sprite sheet like any other, so everything in Limits and build errors applies to it too.

splashpack-cli export <scene> -o <out.splashpack> --stats prints a line for the map when the scene has one:

tilemap 20x15 tile=16x16 sheet=0 objects=2 bytes=632

sheet is the tileset's index among the scene's sprite sheets.

In the scene file the map is the tilemap key, its cells one string a row with the brush index of each cell (-1 empty), so it reads as a grid.

docs.title: The map in the game
docs.text:
The map's top left corner is at pixel 0, 0, and it uses the same pixel space as the sprites: the view offset (Sprite.SetViewOffset) scrolls the map and the sprites together. Lua's x is across the map and z down it: tile column x covers pixels x * tileW to x * tileW + tileW - 1. Tile.MoveActor moves an actor on the world X and Z axes in whole units, so an actor at X = 40, Z = 40 stands in tile 2, 2 of a 16 px map. Off the map is not walkable, so its edge is a wall.

-- Scene script: put a coin sprite on every kind 2 object.
local COIN = 2

function onSceneCreationEnd()
    if not Tile.Active() then return end
    for i = 1, Tile.ObjectCount() do
        local kind, id, x, z = Tile.ObjectAt(i)   -- x, z: the tile's centre in pixels
        if kind == COIN then
            local s = Sprite.Create("coins")
            Sprite.SetPos(s, x - 8, z - 8)         -- SetPos is the top left corner
        end
    end
end

Tile.ObjectAt counts from 1. Loop to Tile.ObjectCount() and do not ask past it: an index out of range returns a value that is not nil. The other functions, with their arguments and what they return without a map, are in the Tile API.

docs.title: Cutscenes & Animations
docs.text:
The Timeline panel animates a scene: moving the camera, objects and lights, showing and hiding UI, filling a progress bar, playing sounds and skinned-mesh clips, rumbling the controller. It docks as a second tab beside the Project panel.

There are two kinds of sequence, built the same way:

Cutscene Animation Played from Lua with Cutscene.Play(name) Animation.Play(name) At a time One Up to 8 Camera tracks Yes No Audio events Yes No

Use a cutscene for a scripted moment that takes over the camera. Use animations for things in the world: a door swinging, a lift, a pulsing light.

docs.title: Opening and creating
docs.text: Open the panel from View > Timeline (it lists every cutscene and animation), or press Edit in timeline next to a sequence in the scene settings under Cutscenes and animations. New cutscene and New animation create one. Double-click the name to rename it; Lua plays it by that name. Names are 1 to 24 characters.

docs.title: The panel
docs.text:
The top bar has the sequence picker (CUTSCENE or ANIMATION and its name), Back to frame 0, Play / Pause (Space), Loop, the current Frame, the Length in frames and its time in seconds, Add track and a button to fit the whole length in the panel. Frames run at 30 per second.

Below, the tracks run down the left and time runs across. The red line is the scrub head. Click or drag in the ruler to scrub: the Scene view poses the cameras, objects, lights and UI at that frame, and restores everything when you stop. Nothing is changed in the scene itself.

docs.title: Tracks
docs.text:
Add track asks for a property and a target. A track drives one property of one target.

Group Properties Target Camera Position, Rotation, H (field of view) none (cutscenes only) Object Position, Rotation, Active, UV Offset An object with a mesh UI Canvas Visible, Element Visible, Progress, Position, Colour A canvas, or canvas/element Light Position, Colour, Intensity, Radius, Enabled An object with a runtime light Rumble Small motor, Large motor none

A sequence has at most 8 tracks, with 64 keys on each. The count shows as TRACKS 5 / 8. Object and light positions must stay within 8 x the scene's GTE scaling of the origin. A track's right-click menu has Remove track and Drive instead, which points the track at another target.

docs.title: Keys
docs.text:
• Double-click a lane to put a key at the scrub head.
  • Drag a key to move it. Drag across lanes to box-select; dragging one moves the selection. Del deletes it.
  • Ctrl+C and Ctrl+V copy keys and paste them at the scrub head.
  • Select a key and the row at the bottom of the panel shows its VALUE and its CURVE: the interpolation from the previous key into this one, Linear, Step, In, Out or In-out. On/off tracks hold each key until the next.

docs.title: Audio and skin events (cutscenes)
docs.text:
Cutscenes also have an EVENTS lane. Audio event plays an audio clip by name at a frame, with a volume and a pan. Skin clip event starts a clip on a skinned object at a frame, looping or not. Animations take skin clip events but no audio.

A cutscene holds at most 64 audio events and 16 skin events, and a scene at most 16 cutscenes.

docs.title: From a script
docs.text:
Cutscene.Play("intro", {
    onComplete = function()
        Scene.Load(1)
    end
})
Animation.Play("lift")

In the block editor, play cutscene does the same. See the Cutscene and Animation APIs.

Export checks

An export stops with an error when a track targets an object, canvas, element or clip that does not exist, or when an animation holds a camera track or an audio event.

docs.title: UI Canvases
docs.text:
A canvas holds the HUD, menus and prompts drawn over the game. The UI tab next to Scene edits them at PS1 resolution (320 x 240), so what you place is where it lands on the console.

A scene can have up to 24 canvases and 256 elements in total (255 in one canvas).

docs.title: The tab
docs.text:
• Canvas picker (top left): the canvas being edited. The menu has New canvas and Delete this canvas; the eye next to it sets whether the canvas is visible when the scene starts.
  • Element list: the canvas's elements. Lower rows draw in front. Use + to add an element, the copy and trash buttons to duplicate and delete, and the arrows to change the order (Ctrl+[ sends backward, Ctrl+] brings forward).
  • Canvas view: the screen. Drag an element to move it, drag its handles to resize it, nudge with the arrow keys. The wheel zooms, middle-drag or Space+drag pans, Ctrl+1 is 100%, Ctrl+0 fits. Ctrl+C, Ctrl+X, Ctrl+V and Ctrl+D copy, cut, paste and duplicate. Hold Ctrl to toggle snapping while dragging.
  • The inspector shows the selected element's properties, with its name at the top (F2 renames the selected row too). With no element selected it shows the canvas's own: its name, Visible and Sort order.

docs.title: Elements
docs.text:
Element Draws Box A solid rectangle Text A line of text: ASCII, at most 63 bytes Image A texture from the project Progress bar A bar filled from 0 to 100 Line A line between two points, with a handle at each end

All elements have a Name (what Lua and timeline tracks find them by), Visible, Position and Size in pixels, an Anchor (what the position stays relative to if the screen size changes; stretched sides follow both edges) and a Colour.

Per type:

  • Text has the Text itself and a Font: the built-in system font (8 x 16, fixed width), or one of the scene's fonts. Fonts live in the scene file; see the scene format notes in the editor's repository. At most 3 fonts per scene.
  • Image has a Texture (Browse copies a file from outside the project into textures/), Native size, Bit depth (4 and 8 bpp use a palette and less VRAM) and Cutout (transparent texels, alpha under half, are left out instead of drawn black). Set Sheet to one of the scene's sprite sheets and the Image shows a single cell instead: click the cell in the picker, and Snap size sets the size to one cell. Renaming the sheet carries the Images along. A Colour of #808080 draws the texture as it is; brighter values brighten it, up to double at white.
  • Progress bar has a Value, 0 to 100.

docs.title: Canvases
docs.text: Visible is whether the canvas shows when the scene starts. Sort order runs from 0 at the back to 255 in front; canvases with higher orders draw over lower ones.

docs.title: Driving the UI
docs.text:
From Lua, find a canvas and an element by name, then change them:

local hud = UI.FindCanvas("hud")
local bar = UI.FindElement(hud, "hp")
UI.SetProgress(bar, 75)
UI.SetText(UI.FindElement(hud, "crates"), "x 3")

Timeline tracks can also animate an element's visibility, position, colour and progress. See the UI API.

docs.title: Prompts and loading screens
docs.text:
• An Interactable can show a canvas as its prompt while the player is in range. The canvas name must fit in 15 characters.
  • A canvas can be the scene's loading screen. The progress bar on it must be named loading.

docs.title: World Streaming
docs.text: A scene can be bigger than the PS1's RAM. With Stream world on, the static level geometry is split into regions that load from the disc as the camera moves and drop again when it moves away. Textures, collision, navigation, scripts and sounds always stay loaded; only triangles stream.

docs.title: Turning it on
docs.text:
Select nothing, and under World streaming switch on Stream world. Everything else is automatic. The section then reports, once the scene exports:

  • the region count and size, and how many objects stream (and how many were cut at region edges),
  • how far from the camera scenery loads,
  • the slots the engine keeps, and the RAM they cost while playing,
  • the RAM saved.

docs.title: Which objects stream
docs.text:
An object streams only if all of these are true:

  • It has triangles.
  • It has no script.
  • It is not skinned.
  • It is not an Interactable.
  • It is not a dynamic collider.
  • No animation or cutscene track moves it.
  • Its name does not appear in any Lua script.

Everything else stays loaded. Large meshes are cut at region edges.

Objects reached by index

The exporter finds script references by name. A script that reaches an object only by index (Entity.FindByIndex) cannot be detected, and the object may be unloaded when the script needs it. Look such objects up by name, or give them a script.

docs.title: Warnings
docs.text:
Warning What to do Nothing can stream Every object is excluded by the rules above. Take scripts off scenery that does not need one, or turn streaming off. Too many pieces to stream The world splits into more than 65535 pieces and exports without streaming. Merge small props. A region is slow to load The biggest region is large. Shorten draw distance lets regions be smaller. One area is much denser Every streaming slot is as big as the biggest region. Spread that area's detail out, or simplify its meshes. Far scenery may appear late More regions are near the camera than the engine keeps. Shorten draw distance. Streaming does not save RAM here Shorten the draw distance, or turn streaming off for this scene. CD music will not play A script calls Audio.PlayCDDA, and a streamed scene keeps the disc drive busy. Use audio clips.

The draw distance is how far the console draws: the ordering table, or the fog wall if fog is on.

docs.title: Output
docs.text: Streaming adds a scene_N.geo file next to the scene's other exported files, and the disc image carries it as SCENE_N.GEO. It works in Play (PCdrv), on hardware and on a disc.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text:
Four steps from download to a disc image:

  1. Installation: download the archive for your OS and unpack it.
  2. Your First Project: open the courtyard example, find your way around, change something.
  3. Play, Hardware and Discs: boot the scene in the emulator, on a real PS1, and as a .bin/.cue disc image.
  4. The Editor: the rest of the interface, one panel at a time.

Nothing else needs installing. The archive carries the editor, the psxsplash engine builds and pcsx-redux.

docs.title: Your First Project
docs.text: The editor opens the courtyard example on first launch: a walled yard with crates, a platform, three lights and a player start. It is a complete scene, so Play works straight away.

docs.title: Work on a copy
docs.text:
The example lives inside the editor folder (examples/courtyard), and updating the editor replaces it. Before you change it, copy the courtyard folder somewhere of your own, then File > Open... (Ctrl+O) and pick courtyard.scene in the copy.

To start from nothing instead, use File > New Project... (Ctrl+N) and pick an empty folder. The editor creates meshes/, textures/ and scripts/ in it and an empty scene named after the folder.

A project is just a folder: one or more .scene files (JSON) and the meshes, textures, scripts and sounds they use, all referenced by paths relative to the folder. Scenes, meshes and block scripts are JSON text, so a project sits well in git.

docs.title: Find your way around
docs.text:
• Scene (left): every object in the scene as a tree. Click to select, double-click to frame, drag to reparent, F2 to rename. The number after a mesh is its triangle count; a warning sign means the inspector has a suggestion.
  • Viewport (middle): the scene drawn at 320x240 with 15-bit colour, dithering and affine texture warping, as the console draws it. Switch to Clean at the top right for a plain view.
  • Inspector (right): the selected object's components. With nothing selected it shows the scene's settings.
  • Project (bottom): the project folder. Drag a file onto the viewport, the scene tree or an inspector field to use it.
  • Status bar: VRAM, SPU RAM, main RAM and triangle counts for the scene as it would export right now.

The interface tour covers each panel in detail.

docs.title: Move around the viewport
docs.text: Input Does Right mouse drag Look around Right mouse + W A S D, Q / E Fly; the wheel changes the speed while flying Middle mouse drag Pan Mouse wheel Move in and out Alt + left drag Orbit Alt + right drag Zoom F Frame the selection

docs.title: Change something
docs.text:
1. Click Crate in the scene tree. The viewport shows a move gizmo on it.
  2. Drag the green arrow up, or type a new Y under Transform > Position in the inspector.
  3. The inspector shows "Texture could be 4 bpp": crate.png has only 7 colours. Click Convert to 4 bpp. The VRAM meter in the status bar drops.
  4. Press Ctrl+S to save.

Every edit is one undo step: Ctrl+Z undoes, Ctrl+Y redoes.

docs.title: Add an object
docs.text:
1. Click + at the top of the Scene panel, or Object > Add Object... (Ctrl+A).
  2. Pick Point light. It appears in front of the camera.
  3. Move it near a wall and set its Colour and Range in the inspector. The PS1 view shows the new baked lighting on the walls around it.

Objects are built from components. Add component at the bottom of the inspector adds more: a Collider, a Script, a Trigger box and so on. See Objects & Components.

docs.title: Add a script
docs.text:
1. Select Game Logic. Its Script component points at scripts/game_logic.lua.
  2. Click Edit script. The file opens in a tab next to Scene, in the Lua editor.
  3. To script with blocks instead, add a Script component to another object and click New blocks; New Lua makes a Lua file. Both are covered in The Block Editor and The Lua Editor.

docs.title: Play it
docs.text:
Press Play in the title bar (F5). The editor exports the scene, boots it in pcsx-redux and shows the game next to the scene view. Click the game to give it the keyboard, then walk with the arrow keys.

Next: Play, Hardware and Discs.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
psxsplash ships as one archive per OS from the nightly release, rebuilt from every change to the editor. Each archive holds:

Folder or file What it is splashedit (splashedit.exe on Windows, SplashEdit.app on macOS) The editor engine/ psxsplash builds: psxsplash.ps-exe for Play and Run on hardware, psxsplash-cdrom.ps-exe for disc images, and builds with debug overlays redux/ pcsx-redux, the emulator Play boots examples/courtyard/ The example project assets/ Fonts and icons the editor uses

Unpack it anywhere and start the editor. Nothing else needs installing. On macOS the other folders sit inside SplashEdit.app.

docs.title: Windows
docs.text:
Windows 10 or later. Download splashedit-windows.zip, extract it, and run splashedit.exe.

The executable is not signed, so SmartScreen may stop the first launch. Click More info, then Run anyway.

docs.title: Linux
docs.text:
x86-64 with glibc 2.38 or newer: Ubuntu 24.04, Debian 13, Fedora 39 and later.

tar xzf splashedit-linux.tar.gz
cd splashedit
./splashedit

./install-desktop-entry.sh adds the editor to your applications menu. Run it again if you move the folder.

docs.title: macOS
docs.text:
Apple silicon only. Download splashedit-macos.tar.gz and unpack it. The app is not notarized, so clear the download quarantine once before the first launch, then open SplashEdit.app:

tar xzf splashedit-macos.tar.gz
xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine splashedit

docs.title: Optional extras
docs.text:
• Blender, to import .blend files directly. The editor runs Blender in the background to read them. It looks for blender on your PATH, then the usual install folders (C:/Program Files/Blender Foundation/ on Windows, /Applications/Blender.app on macOS). Set SPLASHEDIT_BLENDER to the executable to pick one yourself. Every other model format works without it.
  • A BIOS image. pcsx-redux boots with its own BIOS when none is set. To use a real one, pick it under BIOS in the Play setup window (see Play, Hardware and Discs).
  • A serial cable and Unirom on a real console, for Run on hardware.

docs.title: Updating
docs.text: Download the archive again and unpack it over the old folder, or next to it. Projects live in their own folders, so nothing in a project changes when you update the editor.

docs.title: Play, Hardware and Discs
docs.text:
The title bar has the three ways to run a scene: Play, Run on hardware and Export. The Build menu holds the same commands with their shortcuts.

Command Shortcut Runs the scene Play F5 In pcsx-redux, inside the editor Run on Hardware Ctrl+F5 On a PS1 over a serial link Export Disc Image... Ctrl+B As a .bin + .cue disc image

All three save open scripts first and export every scene in the build list. With an empty build list they export the open scene alone.

docs.title: Play
docs.text:
Press Play. The editor exports the scene, boots psxsplash in pcsx-redux, and splits the viewport into Scene and Game, side by side or stacked depending on the window shape. Drag the bar between them to resize.

Click the Game view to give it the keyboard:

Keyboard Controller Arrow keys D-pad Z X A S Cross, Circle, Square, Triangle Q W 1 2 L1, R1, L2, R2 Enter Start Backspace Select

A connected gamepad always drives controller 1, focused or not.

Live edits. The scene stays editable while the game runs. A moment after you stop editing, the editor exports again and the game reloads the scene in place, so you can move a light or retune a player value without restarting.

Output. While the game runs, the status bar shows its state. Click it to see what the game printed, including Debug.Log lines, with a Stop button. Press Play again (it reads Stop now) or F5 to end the game.

docs.title: Setting up the tools
docs.text:
The archive ships everything Play needs, and the editor finds it on its own. If something is missing, the editor opens Set up Play instead of playing:

  • PlayStation executable: the psxsplash build to boot. Defaults to engine/psxsplash.ps-exe.
  • BIOS image: optional. Left empty, pcsx-redux uses its own BIOS.

Locate picks a file. The same window appears as Set up Export for the disc build and Set up Run on hardware for the serial port.

The editor also reads these environment variables, before falling back to the bundled copies: SPLASHEDIT_REDUX, SPLASHEDIT_PSXSPLASH, SPLASHEDIT_BIOS, SPLASHEDIT_DISC_ENGINE and SPLASHEDIT_PORT. If neither is set and no bundled copy is found, it looks for pcsx-redux on your PATH.

docs.title: Debug overlays
docs.text:
Two entries in the Build menu boot a psxsplash build with on-screen diagnostics:

Overlay Shows Performance Overlay FPS counter and a heap bar Room Debug Overlay The room wireframe, for checking rooms and portals

They apply to Play and Run on hardware. Disc images always get the plain CD-ROM build.

docs.title: Run on hardware
docs.text:
Run on hardware uploads psxsplash to a real console and then serves the scene files to it over the same cable, so you can test without burning a disc.

You need:

  • A PS1 running Unirom, sitting at its shell.
  • A serial link: a USB serial adapter wired to the console's serial port, or pcsx-redux's SIO1 server for a dry run.

The first time, Set up Run on hardware asks for the Serial port: COM3 on Windows, /dev/ttyUSB0 on Linux, or tcp:localhost:6699 for pcsx-redux's SIO1 server. Ports found on your machine are listed under Found:. The link runs at 115200 baud.
