Press Run on hardware. The editor exports the scene, sends psxsplash.ps-exe to Unirom, and answers the game's file requests (PCdrv) from the export folder. The status bar shows progress and the game's output, like Play. Stop Hardware Run in the Build menu ends the session.

docs.title: Export a disc image
docs.text:
Press Export (Ctrl+B) and choose where to save the .bin. The editor writes an ISO 9660 image in raw Mode 2 sectors plus its .cue, with the CD-ROM build of psxsplash (engine/psxsplash-cdrom.ps-exe) and every scene in the build list. The status bar reports the file names and size when it is done.

Disc options are in the scene settings under Disc (select nothing to see them):

Field Effect Volume label The disc's volume name, up to 31 characters. Empty uses the scene name. Licence The licence data in the disc's first 16 sectors. None boots in emulators and on modded consoles. psxsplash uses the psxsplash licence; the boot logo reads "Created with psxsplash". Choose file... takes your own licence file. A retail console's BIOS checks this before booting.

The image runs in any PS1 emulator, or burn it to a CD-R for a console that boots burned discs.

No CD-DA tracks

The image holds one data track. Audio.PlayCDDA plays audio tracks from a disc, so it has nothing to play on an editor-made image, nor under Play or Run on hardware, which load files over PCdrv. Use audio clips for music.

docs.title: Lua Scripting
docs.text: Lua runs all game logic in psxsplash. Scripts move objects, show UI, play sounds, run cutscenes and load scenes. You can write the Lua yourself in the Lua editor, or build the same logic from blocks in the block editor, which writes Lua for you. A scene can mix both.

docs.title: This is not standard Lua
docs.text:
The Lua VM on the PS1 uses fixed-point numbers instead of floating-point. The PS1 has no floating-point hardware. This changes how you write math:

  • There are no decimal literals. 0.5 does not exist.
  • Integer division gives integers. 1/2 equals 0, not 0.5.
  • Use FixedPoint.new() for fractional values. It is the only way to get a non-integer number.

Read Fixed-Point Math before writing scripts. Blocks do this for you: type 0.5 into a block and the generated Lua uses FixedPoint.new.

docs.title: Where scripts go
docs.text:
There are three places a script attaches, and each has its own events.

Script Set in the editor Gets Scene script Scene settings, Script > File (select nothing to see them) onSceneCreationStart, onSceneCreationEnd. Runs once at scene load. A good place for shared functions and game state. Object script Script component on an object onCreate, onUpdate, onInteract, onCollideWithPlayer, onButtonPress and the rest of the object events Trigger script Script field of a Trigger box component onTriggerEnter(index), onTriggerExit(index)

A file is either .lua or .blocks; the extension decides which. New Lua and New blocks in the inspector create one in scripts/ named after the object and open it. Press Play and the scene runs with your changes.

docs.title: Script environments
docs.text:
Each script runs in its own environment. Functions defined in one script are NOT automatically available to other scripts. To share functions (for example, from the scene script to object scripts), publish them to _G:

-- In the scene script
function addScore(amount)
    -- ...
end

-- Publish so object scripts can call it
_G.addScore = addScore

Then any object script can call addScore(100) directly, because _G is the fallback for all environments.

docs.title: In this section
docs.text:
1. Fixed-Point Math: how numbers work on the PS1. Read this first.
  2. Event Callbacks: every callback and when it fires.
  3. API Reference: every Lua function the engine provides.
  4. Patterns: working code for common game mechanics.

docs.title: Lua API Reference
docs.text:
Every function the engine gives your Lua scripts, as of the current psxsplash source. Numbers that carry fractions are fixed-point.

Not listed: the Net table. The engine has it, but the editor has no way to author a network link yet.

docs.title: Entity
docs.text: Manage game objects in the scene.

docs.title: Finding Objects
docs.text:
Entity.Find(name)
Find an object by its name in the scene tree (string). Returns the object or nil.

Entity.FindByIndex(index)
Find an object by its array index (0-based). Returns the object or nil.

Entity.FindByScriptIndex(index)
Find the first object with a matching Lua script file index. Returns the object or nil.

Entity.GetCount()
Returns the total number of objects in the scene.

Entity.ForEach(callback)
Iterate all active objects. The callback receives (object, index) for each. Skips inactive objects.

Entity.ForEach(function(obj, i)
    Debug.Log("Object " .. i .. " is active")
end)

docs.title: Active State
docs.text:
Entity.SetActive(object, bool)
Show or hide an object. Fires onEnable or onDisable callbacks.

Entity.IsActive(object)
Returns true if the object is active.

docs.title: Position
docs.text:
Entity.GetPosition(object)
Returns a Vec3 table {x, y, z} in world coordinates.

Entity.SetPosition(object, vec3)
Set position instantly (no physics, no interpolation).

-- Example
local pos = Entity.GetPosition(self)
Entity.SetPosition(self, Vec3.new(pos.x + 1, pos.y, pos.z))

docs.title: Rotation
docs.text:
Entity.GetRotationY(object)
Get the Y-axis rotation as an angle in pi-units.

Entity.SetRotationY(object, angle)
Set the Y-axis rotation. Angle is in pi-units (1 = 180 degrees, FixedPoint.new(1) / 2 = 90 degrees).

Entity.SetRotation(object, vec3)
Set the full rotation from a Vec3 of Euler angles {x, y, z} in pi-units. Applied as a Y * X * Z rotation matrix (same convention as Camera.SetRotation).

docs.title: Direction Vectors
docs.text:
Get an object's local axes in world space, derived from its current rotation. Each returns a Vec3 {x, y, z}.

Entity.GetForward(object)   -- local +Z in world space
Entity.GetRight(object)     -- local +X in world space
Entity.GetUp(object)        -- local +Y in world space

-- Spawn something 2 units in front of an object
local fwd = Entity.GetForward(self)
local pos = Entity.GetPosition(self)
local spawnPos = Vec3.add(pos, Vec3.mul(fwd, FixedPoint.new(2)))

docs.title: Local Movement
docs.text:
Move an object along its own local axes (relative to its rotation), by a fixed-point step. These are convenience wrappers over GetForward/GetRight/GetUp + SetPosition.

Entity.MoveForward(object, step)
Entity.MoveBackward(object, step)
Entity.MoveLeft(object, step)
Entity.MoveRight(object, step)
Entity.MoveUp(object, step)
Entity.MoveDown(object, step)

-- Drive an object forward along its facing each frame
function onUpdate(self, dt)
    Entity.MoveForward(self, FixedPoint.new(1) / 32)
end

No collision

Like SetPosition, these move the transform directly - they ignore navigation regions and collision. They affect the object, not the player.

docs.title: Texture Manipulation
docs.text:
Change how an object's polygons are textured at runtime. Useful for scrolling textures, sprite-sheet animation, and swapping texture pages.

Entity.SetUVOffset(object, u, v)
Set an absolute UV offset (0-255 each) applied non-destructively at render time. The source polygon UVs are left untouched, so you can animate this freely every frame. This is the same value driven by the UV Offset timeline track.

Entity.SetUVs(object, {u, v})
Additively shift the UVs of every polygon on the object by (u, v). Unlike SetUVOffset, this mutates the stored polygon UVs, so repeated calls accumulate.

Entity.SetTPage(object, {x, y})
Set the texture page (VRAM page coordinates) for every polygon on the object - effectively swapping which region of VRAM it samples from.

-- Scroll a texture horizontally (e.g. a waterfall or conveyor belt)
local scroll = 0
function onUpdate(self, dt)
    scroll = (scroll + 1) % 256
    Entity.SetUVOffset(self, scroll, 0)
end

docs.title: Parenting
docs.text:
Entity.SetParent(parent, child, offset)
Snap child to parent: the child is placed at the parent's position plus offset (a Vec3 expressed in the parent's local space) and inherits the parent's rotation. This is a one-shot reparent each call - to keep a child attached, call it every frame in onUpdate.

-- Keep a "held item" attached to a character's hand bone offset
function onUpdate(self, dt)
    local hand = Entity.Find("Character")
    Entity.SetParent(hand, self, Vec3.new(FixedPoint.new(0), FixedPoint.new(1), FixedPoint.new(0)))
end

The scene tree is flattened at export, so a parent in the editor does not carry its children along. Entity.SetParent is how you attach at runtime.

docs.title: Self Properties
docs.text:
Object scripts have shorthand access via self:

self.position      -- {x, y, z} (read/write)
self.active        -- boolean (read/write)
self.rotation      -- {x, y, z} (read/write)
self.rotationY     -- angle in pi-units (read/write)

docs.title: Vec3
docs.text:
3D vector math. All functions return new tables.

Vec3.new(x, y, z)          -- Create vector
Vec3.add(a, b)              -- a + b
Vec3.sub(a, b)              -- a - b
Vec3.mul(v, scalar)         -- v * scalar
Vec3.dot(a, b)              -- Dot product (scalar)
Vec3.cross(a, b)            -- Cross product (vector)
Vec3.length(v)              -- Magnitude ||v||
Vec3.lengthSq(v)            -- Squared magnitude (faster, no sqrt)
Vec3.normalize(v)           -- Unit vector (length = 1)
Vec3.distance(a, b)         -- Distance between two points
Vec3.distanceSq(a, b)       -- Squared distance (faster)
Vec3.lerp(a, b, t)          -- Linear interpolation: a + (b-a)*t

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
local a = Vec3.new(1, 0, 0)
local b = Vec3.new(0, 1, 0)

local sum = Vec3.add(a, b)           -- {1, 1, 0}
local cross = Vec3.cross(a, b)       -- {0, 0, 1}
local dot = Vec3.dot(a, b)           -- 0
local one = FixedPoint.new(1)
local mid = Vec3.lerp(a, b, one / 2) -- {0.5, 0.5, 0}
local dist = Vec3.distance(a, b)     -- ~1.41

Use squared versions for comparisons

Vec3.distanceSq and Vec3.lengthSq avoid a square root. If you're comparing distances (e.g., "is the player within range?"), compare squared distances instead.

docs.title: Input
docs.text: Controller button constants and state queries.

docs.title: Button Constants
docs.text:
Input.CROSS          Input.CIRCLE         Input.SQUARE         Input.TRIANGLE
Input.L1             Input.L2             Input.R1             Input.R2
Input.START          Input.SELECT
Input.UP             Input.DOWN           Input.LEFT           Input.RIGHT
Input.L3             Input.R3

docs.title: State Queries
docs.text:
Two-player API change

State queries are per-player. Player 1 reads the controller in port 1, player 2 reads port 2. The old single-controller names (Input.IsPressed, Input.IsReleased, Input.IsHeld, Input.GetAnalog) were removed - use the Player1 / Player2 variants below. If you only support one player, use the Player1 functions.

Input.IsPressedPlayer1(button)
Input.IsPressedPlayer2(button)
Returns true only on the frame the button was pressed (edge trigger).

Input.IsReleasedPlayer1(button)
Input.IsReleasedPlayer2(button)
Returns true only on the frame the button was released.

Input.IsHeldPlayer1(button)
Input.IsHeldPlayer2(button)
Returns true every frame while the button is held down.

Input.GetAnalogPlayer1(stick)
Input.GetAnalogPlayer2(stick)
Read analog stick position. stick 0 = left stick, 1 = right stick. Returns two values: x, y in range -127 to +127 (0 = centered).

-- Player 1, left stick
local x, y = Input.GetAnalogPlayer1(0)

-- Simple two-player check
if Input.IsPressedPlayer1(Input.CROSS) then jump(1) end
if Input.IsPressedPlayer2(Input.CROSS) then jump(2) end

Button events fire for both players

The onButtonPress / onButtonRelease object callbacks fire for presses on either controller. They receive only the button id, not the player number - if you need to tell players apart, poll Input.*Player1 / Input.*Player2 directly (e.g. in onUpdate).

docs.title: Driving something other than the player
docs.text:
Input.BindToActor(player, actor)
Point a controller's built-in locomotion at any actor. player is 1 or 2. The pad then walks and turns that actor with the engine's normal movement, collision and camera handling, instead of the scene's Player.

Input.GetBoundActor(player)   -- -> actor id as a plain number

-- hand pad 1 back to the player
Input.BindToActor(1, Actor.GetPlayer())

Binding is how you build local co-op or possessable NPCs.

GetBoundActor returns an id, not a handle

It gives you the actor index as a number. Pass it through Actor.FindByIndex before calling any other Actor.* function on it.

docs.title: Camera
docs.text:
Control the scene camera.

Camera.FollowPsxPlayer(bool)
Sets if the camera should be controlled by the Player. Set false if you want to use the lua functions below to control the camera. 

Camera.GetPosition()
Returns the camera's world position as vec3 {x, y, z}.

Camera.SetPosition(x, y, z)
Camera.SetPosition(vec3) -- {x, y, z}
Set camera position. Accepts three numbers or a vec3 table.

Camera.GetRotation()
Returns the camera's world rotation as Vec3 {x, y, z}

Camera.SetRotation(vec3)
Set camera rotation in pi-units. Applied as Y * X * Z rotation matrix. Accepts Vec3

Camera.MoveForward(stepAmount)
Moves the camera forward based on it's rotation and a fixed point number stepAmount

Camera.MoveBackward(stepAmount)
Moves the camera backward based on it's rotation and a fixed point number stepAmount

Camera.MoveLeft(stepAmount)
Moves the camera left based on it's rotation and a fixed point number stepAmount

Camera.MoveRight(stepAmount)
Moves the camera right based on it's rotation and a fixed point number stepAmount

Camera.GetForward()
Returns the camera's forward vector as Vec3 {x, y, z}

Camera.GetH()
Returns the current projection plane distance (H register). Default is 120. Higher values = narrower FOV (more telephoto), lower = wider FOV.

Camera.SetH(h)
Set the projection H register. Clamped to 1-1024. Use this to change the field of view at runtime.

The relationship between H and vertical FOV is: $\text{vFOV} = 2 \cdot \arctan\left(\frac{120}{H}\right)$

H Approx. Vertical FOV 60 ~127° (ultra wide) 120 ~90° (default) 200 ~62° 400 ~33° (telephoto)

docs.title: Following an actor
docs.text:
Camera.SetFollowTarget(actor)
Point the follow camera at any actor instead of the player. The camera keeps its usual orbit behaviour; only the thing it orbits changes.

Camera.GetFollowTarget()   -- -> actor handle, or nil if following nothing
Camera.ClearFollowTarget() -- stop following; the camera holds its last transform

This is how you hand the camera to a vehicle or a spectator target.

Navigation controller override

In scenes with a Player and navigation regions, the navigation controller continuously overrides camera position and rotation. Manual camera changes via these functions will be overwritten on the next frame. The Camera API is primarily useful during cutscenes, which temporarily suspend the navigation controller.

Camera.LookAt(x, y, z)
Camera.LookAt(vec3)
Turn the camera toward a world point. It sets the camera's rotation once; call it each frame to keep tracking.

Check out the example script

"Lua Free Cam" in the patterns section uses these camera functions.

docs.title: Player
docs.text:
Control the player.

Player.GetPosition()
Returns the player's position as Vec3 {x, y, z}.

Player.SetPosition(x, y, z)
Player.SetPosition(Vec3) -- {x, y, z}
Set player position. Accepts three numbers or a Vec3 table.

Player.GetRotation()
Returns the player's rotation as Vec3 {x, y, z}

Player.SetRotation(Vec3)
Set players rotation. Accepts Vec3

Check out the example script

"Player Position and Rotation" in Patterns.

docs.title: UI
docs.text: Canvas and element manipulation. Canvases and their elements are built in the UI canvas editor.

docs.title: Canvas Operations
docs.text:
UI.FindCanvas(name)                      -- Find canvas by name -> index or -1
UI.SetCanvasVisible(nameOrIndex, bool)   -- Show/hide (accepts name string or index number)
UI.IsCanvasVisible(nameOrIndex)          -- Check visibility -> boolean

docs.title: Element Lookup
docs.text:
UI.FindElement(canvasIndex, name)        -- Find element by name -> handle or -1
UI.GetElementCount(canvasIndex)          -- Number of elements in canvas
UI.GetElementByIndex(canvasIndex, i)     -- Get element by position -> handle
UI.GetElementType(handle)               -- 0=Image, 1=Box, 2=Text, 3=Progress, 4=Line

docs.title: Visibility
docs.text:
UI.SetVisible(handle, bool)
UI.IsVisible(handle)

docs.title: Text
docs.text:
UI.SetText(handle, text)                -- Max 63 characters
UI.GetText(handle)                      -- Returns string

docs.title: Progress Bar
docs.text:
UI.SetProgress(handle, value)            -- 0-100 (clamped)
UI.GetProgress(handle)                   -- Returns number

docs.title: Sheet Cell
docs.text:
An Image backed by a sprite sheet cell (set in the editor's Sheet field) can show another cell of the same sheet:

UI.SetFrame(handle, cell)                -- cell 0-255, row by row from the top left
UI.GetFrame(handle)                      -- Returns the cell, or -1 for a plain Image

SetFrame does nothing on an Image that is not backed by a sheet.

docs.title: Color
docs.text:
UI.SetColor(handle, r, g, b)            -- RGB 0-255
UI.GetColor(handle)                     -- Returns r, g, b (three values)
UI.SetProgressColors(handle, bgR, bgG, bgB, fillR, fillG, fillB)

docs.title: Position & Size
docs.text:
UI.SetPosition(handle, x, y)
UI.GetPosition(handle)                   -- Returns x, y
UI.SetSize(handle, w, h)
UI.GetSize(handle)                       -- Returns w, h

These are ANCHOR-relative, not screen coordinates

x and y are the element's offset from its anchor, which is what the splashpack stores; the runtime adds the anchor's own position when it draws. For a centre-anchored canvas on a 320x240 display that is a (160, 120) difference. GetPosition and SetPosition speak the same space, so reading a position and writing it back is exact - but passing a screen coordinate to SetPosition is not.

docs.title: Immediate-Mode Drawing
docs.text:
Draw primitives straight to the GPU this frame, without any pre-authored element. Coordinates are PS1 screen pixels (320x240); colors are RGB 0-255. Call these from onUpdate to keep them on screen - they are not persistent and must be re-issued every frame.

UI.DrawLine(p1, p2, color)
Draw a single-pixel gouraud line from p1 to p2. Each argument is a 2- or 3-element array table: {x, y} for the points, {r, g, b} for the color.

UI.DrawTriangle(p1, p2, p3, c1, c2, c3)
Draw a filled gouraud triangle. p1/p2/p3 are {x, y} points; c1/c2/c3 are per-vertex {r, g, b} colors (the fill is smoothly interpolated between them).

function onUpdate(self, dt)
    -- A red line across the screen
    UI.DrawLine({10, 120}, {310, 120}, {255, 0, 0})

    -- A triangle with a different color at each corner
    UI.DrawTriangle(
        {160, 40}, {120, 120}, {200, 120},
        {255, 0, 0}, {0, 255, 0}, {0, 0, 255})
end

Drawn on top, every frame

These primitives are sent immediately and are not depth-sorted with your scene. Because they don't persist, you must call them each frame you want them visible. Pair with PSXMath.Convert3DTo2D to anchor them to world objects.

docs.title: Audio
docs.text:
Play sound effects and music. Clips are set up with an Audio clip component.

Audio.Play(nameOrIndex, volume, pan)
Play a clip. Returns channel number (0-23) or -1 if all voices busy.

  • nameOrIndex: clip name (string) or index (number)
  • volume: 0-128 (default 100)
  • pan: 0-127, where 0=left, 64=center, 127=right (default 64)
Audio.Find(name)         -- Find clip by name -> index or nil
Audio.Stop(channel)      -- Stop a specific channel
Audio.SetVolume(channel, volume, pan)  -- Adjust mid-playback
Audio.StopAll()          -- Stop all channels

docs.title: CD-DA Playback
docs.text:
Play music tracks burned onto the disc as CD-DA audio. CD-DA only works when running from a disc image, and the editor writes no CD-DA tracks into the images it makes (see Audio). Track numbers start at 2 because track 1 is the data track.

Audio.PlayCDDA(trackNo)
Start playing a CD-DA audio track by track number.

Audio.PauseCDDA()
Pause the currently playing CD-DA track.

Audio.ResumeCDDA()
Resume a paused CD-DA track.

Audio.StopCDDA()
Stop CD-DA playback entirely.

Audio.TellCDDA(callback)
Query the current playback position. The result is returned asynchronously through a callback function. The callback receives a single fixed-point value representing the playback position in seconds.

Audio.TellCDDA(function(position)
    Debug.Log("CD-DA position: " .. position)
end)


Audio.SetCDDAVolume(left, right)
Set the CD-DA output volume for left and right channels independently.

No CD-DA from the editor

CD-DA needs audio tracks on the disc. Play and Run on hardware load files over PCdrv, and the disc image the editor writes has one data track. Use audio clips for music. A scene with world streaming on ignores Audio.PlayCDDA as well.

docs.title: Light
docs.text:
Control runtime point lights. Only lights marked runtime in the scene exist at runtime; baked lights are part of the vertex colours and cannot be found. See Lighting.

Light.Find(name)
Find a light by its object name. Returns a light handle (a number), or nil if there is no such light.

Light.SetPosition(light, vec3)
Move a light. Takes a Vec3 table {x, y, z} in world coordinates, the same units as Entity.SetPosition.

Light.SetColor(light, r, g, b)           -- RGB 0-255 (clamped)
Light.SetRadius(light, radius)           -- same units as positions; light fades to zero at this distance
Light.SetIntensity(light, intensity)     -- 1.0 = normal brightness
Light.SetEnabled(light, enabled)         -- true / false

-- A torch that follows an object
local torch = Light.Find("Torch")

function onUpdate(self, dt)
    Light.SetPosition(torch, Entity.GetPosition(self))
end

Light functions do nothing if the handle is not a valid light.

docs.title: Scene
docs.text:
Multi-scene management.

Scene.Load(sceneIndex)
Request a scene transition. The load is deferred to end-of-frame - code after this call still executes.

Scene.GetIndex()
Returns the current scene's index (0-based, the position in the build list).

docs.title: Persist
docs.text:
Cross-scene persistent data storage. Survives scene loads but is lost on power-off.

Persist.Set(key, value)   -- Store a number with a string key
Persist.Get(key)          -- Retrieve -> number or nil if not set

Limits

Maximum 16 key-value pairs. Values are numbers only. Silently fails if the table is full.

RAM vs. memory card

Persist keeps data only until power-off. To write a real save that survives a reboot and shows up in the BIOS, use MemCard.

docs.title: MemCard
docs.text:
Read and write real saves on a physical (or emulated) PlayStation memory card. Unlike Persist, these survive power-off and appear in the BIOS memory card manager. See Scene Settings for project setup (region/product code, save title, BIOS icon).

port is 0 (slot 1) or 1 (slot 2). Every function returns two values: a result and an error string. On success the error is nil; on failure the result is false/nil and the error is a human-readable message - nothing fails silently.

Blocking operations

Saving, loading, formatting and listing block for the duration of the card access (tens of milliseconds, occasionally more). Do them at deliberate save points, never every frame.

docs.title: MemCard.IsPresent
docs.text:
local present, err = MemCard.IsPresent(0)
Returns whether a card is inserted in the given port. (Absence is reported via present == false, not as an error.)

docs.title: MemCard.Save
docs.text:
local ok, err = MemCard.Save(port, key, table)
local ok, err = MemCard.Save(port, key, table, title)
Serialize a Lua table and write it as a save named key. Optional title overrides the project's configured BIOS title for this save.

Supported value types inside the table: nil, booleans, integers, strings, nested tables, and FixedPoint values. Functions, threads and other userdata cause an error. Tables may nest up to 16 levels deep (cycles are rejected).

local ok, err = MemCard.Save(0, "slot1", {
    level = 3,
    hp = FixedPoint.new(100),
    name = "HERO",
    flags = { door1 = true, bossDead = false },
})
if not ok then Debug.Log("Save failed: " .. err) end

docs.title: MemCard.Load
docs.text:
local data, err = MemCard.Load(port, key)
Load and deserialize a save. Returns the reconstructed table (with the same value types you saved) or nil plus an error if the save is missing or corrupt.

local data, err = MemCard.Load(0, "slot1")
if data then
    Persist.Set("level", Convert.FpToInt(data.hp))  -- example
    Debug.Log("Loaded " .. data.name)
end

docs.title: MemCard.Delete
docs.text:
local ok, err = MemCard.Delete(port, key)
Delete a save by key.

docs.title: MemCard.List
docs.text:
local names, err = MemCard.List(port)
Return an array of file names on the card (up to 15). Useful for showing existing saves or checking whether a slot is taken.

docs.title: MemCard.FreeBlocks
docs.text:
local blocks, err = MemCard.FreeBlocks(port)
Return the number of free 8 KiB blocks on the card (a standard card has 15). Check this before saving to a near-full card.

docs.title: MemCard.Format
docs.text:
local ok, err = MemCard.Format(port)
Write a fresh, empty Sony filesystem to the card. Erases everything on the card - only offer this behind an explicit "format card" confirmation.

docs.title: Cutscene
docs.text:
Control cutscene playback. Only one at a time. Cutscenes are built in the timeline.

Cutscene.Play(name)
Cutscene.Play(name, {
    loop = true,               -- Loop the cutscene
    onComplete = function()    -- Called when cutscene ends (not per-loop)
        -- ...
    end
})
Cutscene.Stop()                -- Stop current cutscene
Cutscene.IsPlaying()           -- Check if any cutscene is playing -> boolean

docs.title: Animation
docs.text:
Control animation playback. Multiple simultaneous instances. Animations are built in the timeline.

Animation.Play(name)
Animation.Play(name, {
    loop = true,
    onComplete = function()
        -- ...
    end
})
Animation.Stop(name)           -- Stop all instances of named animation
Animation.Stop()               -- Stop ALL animations
Animation.IsPlaying(name)     -- True if any instance is active -> boolean

docs.title: SkinnedAnim
docs.text:
Control bone-based skinned mesh animations. See Skinned Animation.

Each skinned object can play one clip at a time. Clips are referenced by the object name (the object with the Skinned animation component) and the clip name (the name inside the .anim file, which is the animation's name in the model file).

docs.title: SkinnedAnim.Play
docs.text:
SkinnedAnim.Play(objectName, clipName)
SkinnedAnim.Play(objectName, clipName, {
    loop = true,                -- Loop the animation (default: false)
    onComplete = function()     -- Called when a non-looping clip finishes
        -- ...
    end
})

Start playing a skinned animation clip. If the object is already playing, the new clip replaces it immediately.

-- Play idle loop
SkinnedAnim.Play("MyCharacter", "idle", { loop = true })

-- Play attack, then return to idle
SkinnedAnim.Play("MyCharacter", "attack", {
    onComplete = function()
        SkinnedAnim.Play("MyCharacter", "idle", { loop = true })
    end
})

docs.title: SkinnedAnim.Stop
docs.text:
SkinnedAnim.Stop(objectName)

Stop the skinned animation on the given object. The mesh freezes at its current pose. Also releases any onComplete callback.

docs.title: SkinnedAnim.IsPlaying
docs.text:
SkinnedAnim.IsPlaying(objectName) -- -> boolean

Returns true if the named skinned object is currently playing an animation.

docs.title: SkinnedAnim.GetClip
docs.text:
SkinnedAnim.GetClip(objectName) -- -> string or nil

Returns the name of the currently active clip, or nil if the object is not playing or not found.

local clip = SkinnedAnim.GetClip("MyCharacter")
if clip == "idle" then
    SkinnedAnim.Play("MyCharacter", "walk", { loop = true })
end

docs.title: SkinnedAnim.GetBone
docs.text:
local pos, rot = SkinnedAnim.GetBone(objectName, bone)  -- bone: name or index

Returns where a bone is right now: its world position as a Vec3, and its world rotation as a Vec3 (the same convention as Entity.GetRotation). Returns nil if the object is not skinned or the bone does not exist. Use it to attach a weapon or an effect to a hand.

local hand = SkinnedAnim.GetBone("Hero", "hand_r")
if hand then Entity.SetPosition(Entity.Find("Sword"), hand) end

docs.title: Controls
docs.text:
Enable/disable player movement input, per player.

Two-player API change

These are now per-player, matching the Input split. The old Controls.SetEnabled / Controls.IsEnabled names were removed. For a single-player game use the Player1 variants.

Controls.SetEnabledPlayer1(bool)   -- true = player 1 can move, false = frozen
Controls.SetEnabledPlayer2(bool)   -- player 2 (controller port 2)
Controls.IsEnabledPlayer1()        -- Check state -> boolean
Controls.IsEnabledPlayer2()        -- Check state -> boolean

Use this during cutscenes, dialogue, or any time the player shouldn't move. Disabling controls only freezes built-in movement/look - button event callbacks still fire, so menus and dialogue advancement keep working.

-- Freeze everyone for a cutscene
Controls.SetEnabledPlayer1(false)
Controls.SetEnabledPlayer2(false)

Built-in movement is shared

The engine's built-in player movement responds to both controller ports moving the same player (so a second pad acts as a co-pilot). These toggles enable/disable each port's contribution to that movement. For genuinely independent two-player gameplay, disable the built-in movement and drive a second character yourself from the Input.*Player2 functions plus Entity movement.

docs.title: Interact
docs.text:
Enable/disable interaction on specific objects.

Interact.SetEnabled(object, bool)    -- Enable/disable + hide prompt
Interact.IsEnabled(object)           -- Check state -> boolean

docs.title: Timer
docs.text:
Frame counting.

Timer.GetFrameCount()
Returns the number of frames since the current scene loaded. Resets to 0 on each scene load.

docs.title: PSXMath
docs.text:
Integer math utilities.

PSXMath.Clamp(value, min, max)     -- Clamp to range
PSXMath.Lerp(a, b, t)             -- Linear interpolation: a + (b-a)*t
PSXMath.Sign(value)                -- Returns -1, 0, or 1
PSXMath.Abs(value)                 -- Absolute value
PSXMath.Min(a, b)                  -- Minimum
PSXMath.Max(a, b)                  -- Maximum

All operate on fixed-point numbers. Use FixedPoint.new(1) / 2 for fractional arguments like t in Lerp.

docs.title: Trigonometry
docs.text:
PSXMath.Cos(degrees)               -- Cosine, angle in DEGREES (0-360)
PSXMath.Sin(degrees)               -- Sine, angle in DEGREES (0-360)

These take the angle in degrees (a plain integer, not pi-units) and return a fixed-point value using the PS1's hardware trig tables. Convenient for circular/oscillating motion:

-- Bob an object up and down
function onUpdate(self, dt)
    local t = Timer.GetFrameCount() * 4   -- degrees per frame
    local pos = Entity.GetPosition(self)
    Entity.SetPosition(self, Vec3.new(pos.x, PSXMath.Sin(t % 360), pos.z))
end

docs.title: Projection
docs.text:
PSXMath.Convert3DTo2D(vec3)        -- Returns screenX, screenY (two numbers)
Project a 3D world position through the current camera to 2D screen coordinates (320x240 space). Returns two numbers. Useful for pinning UI or immediate-mode lines onto a moving 3D object - for example, drawing a marker over an enemy's head.

local enemy = Entity.Find("Enemy")
local p = Entity.GetPosition(enemy)
local sx, sy = PSXMath.Convert3DTo2D(p)
UI.DrawLine({sx - 4, sy}, {sx + 4, sy}, {255, 0, 0})

docs.title: Random
docs.text:
Accepts integers and generates random numbers for simulating dice, decks of cards, luck mechanics, etc. The functions Random.Number and Random.Range are generated based on the time. If you want to get the same sequence of numbers every time based on a seed use Random.GeneratorSeed, Random.GeneratorNumber, and Random.GeneratorRange.

Random.Number(max)
Returns from 1 to max inclusive.

Random.Range(min,max)
Returns from min inclusive to max inclusive 

Random.GeneratorSeed(newSeed)
Sets the seed for the random number generator. 

Random.GeneratorNumber(max)
Returns from 1 to max inclusive

Random.GeneratorRange(min,max)
Returns from min inclusive to max inclusive

docs.title: FixedPoint
docs.text:
Create fixed-point numbers explicitly.

FixedPoint.new(integer)
Creates a fixed-point value from an integer. FixedPoint.new(1) = 1.0.

Useful for creating precise step sizes:

local one = FixedPoint.new(1)
local step = one / 64   -- Very small step (~0.015)

docs.title: Convert
docs.text:
Helper functions for working with fixed-point numbers. The raw integer of fixed point 1 equals 4096. 

Convert.FpToInt(fixedPoint)

Returns the raw integer representation of the passed fixed point value.

Convert.IntToFp(integer);

Returns the fixed point representation of the passed integer.

docs.title: Expected Conversions
docs.text: Fixed Point Raw Int 1.0 4096 0.5 2048 0.25 1024

docs.title: Debug
docs.text:
Development tools.

Debug.Log(message)
Print to the console. Visible in PCSX-Redux stdout when running on emulator.

Debug.DrawLine(fromVec3, toVec3 [, colorVec3])
Debug.DrawBox(centerVec3, sizeVec3 [, colorVec3])

The draw calls are accepted but nothing is drawn

Both functions validate their arguments and return without queueing anything. They are safe to leave in a script - they simply have no visible effect yet. See Known Issues.

docs.title: Actor
docs.text:
An actor is a movable thing with a position and rotation: the player, or any scene object you address by name. Actor handles are what Input.BindToActor and the camera follow functions take.

Actor handles are not Entity handles

Entity.* functions take an object handle from Entity.Find; Actor.* functions take an actor handle from Actor.Find. Calling Entity.GetPosition on an actor handle returns nil rather than raising, so the mistake shows up later as a nil-index error somewhere unrelated. Use Actor.GetEntity(actor) to cross over deliberately.

docs.title: Finding actors
docs.text:
Actor.GetPlayer()         -- the player's actor
Actor.Find(name)          -- by object name -> actor or nil
Actor.FindByIndex(index)  -- by actor id -> actor or nil
Actor.GetCount()          -- how many actors the scene has
Actor.IsPlayer(actor)     -- true if this is the player
Actor.GetName(actor)      -- object name -> string or nil
Actor.GetEntity(actor)    -- the matching Entity handle, for Entity.* calls

docs.title: Position and rotation
docs.text:
Actor.GetPosition(actor)          -- -> {x, y, z} of FixedPoint
Actor.SetPosition(actor, vec3)
Actor.GetRotation(actor)          -- -> {x, y, z}
Actor.SetRotation(actor, vec3)


local x, z = Actor.GetPositionXZ(actor)
The same position as two plain integers, in pixels, on the ground plane.

Prefer GetPositionXZ in per-frame code

GetPosition builds four Lua tables per call (the vector, plus a FixedPoint for each component). Called for every actor every frame that is thousands of short-lived tables a second for the collector to deal with on a 33MHz CPU. GetPositionXZ allocates nothing.

docs.title: Navigation
docs.text:
Actor.GetNavRegion(actor)         -- current nav region index, or nil
Actor.FindPath(actor, x, y, z)    -- path to a point

docs.title: Agent
docs.text: Agents are objects with an Agent (NPC) component (see Agents): the engine walks them along the nav regions, patrols their waypoints and checks what they see and hear. Every function takes an actor handle: self in the agent's own script, or Actor.Find(name). Positions are {x, y, z} tables in engine units (scene metres divided by the GTE scaling), Y down, like Actor.GetPosition. The engine runs agents only in a scene with nav regions.

docs.title: Enabling and moving
docs.text:
Agent.IsAgent(actor)  -- -> bool
True if the object has an Agent component, or was moved by MoveTo or SetTarget.

Agent.SetEnabled(actor, bool)
Turns the agent on or off. Off stops it where it is and drops its target.

Agent.IsEnabled(actor)  -- -> bool
Whether the agent is running.

Agent.MoveTo(actor, vec3)
Walks to a position along the nav regions; pass another actor instead of a position to follow it. Enables the agent first. In the Patrol state the next waypoint is picked again whenever a move ends.

Agent.SetTarget(actor, target)
Follows another actor (Actor.GetPlayer() for the player); it is also who the agent watches and listens for. Enables the agent first.

Agent.GetTarget(actor)  -- -> actor or nil
The actor it follows, or nil.

Agent.Stop(actor)
Stops moving and drops the target.

Agent.IsMoving(actor)  -- -> bool
Whether it is walking somewhere.

Agent.SetSpeed(actor, speed)
Walking speed per frame, in engine units (a FixedPoint).

Agent.GetSpeed(actor)  -- -> number
Walking speed per frame as a whole number of engine units: see the warning below.

docs.title: State machine
docs.text:
Agent.GetState(actor)  -- -> state
The state number: 0 Idle, 1 Patrol, 2 Seek, 3 Flee, 4 Attack, 5 Wander, 6 Investigate, 7 Custom.

Agent.SetState(actor, state)
Changes the state: runs onStateExit and onStateEnter on the agent's script and plays the state's skin clip when one is set.

docs.title: Senses
docs.text:
Agent.CanSee(actor, target)  -- -> bool
True when target is inside the vision range and cone and within the region hops. Ranges are measured as the larger of the X and Z distances, so they are squares, not circles.

Agent.CanHear(actor, target)  -- -> bool
True when target is inside the hearing range (a square, like the vision range).

Agent.SetVisionRange(actor, range)
Vision range in engine units; 0 sees nothing.

Agent.GetVisionRange(actor)  -- -> number
Vision range as a whole number of engine units: see the warning below.

Agent.SetVisionAngle(actor, deg)
HALF the cone in degrees, 0 to 180 (the inspector's Field of view is the whole cone); 180 sees all around.

Agent.SetHearingRange(actor, range)
Hearing range in engine units; 0 hears nothing.

Agent.GetHearingRange(actor)  -- -> number
Hearing range as a whole number of engine units: see the warning below.

Agent.SetAlertTimeout(actor, frames)
Frames after it last sensed the target before onTargetLost runs.

Agent.GetLastKnownPos(actor)  -- -> {x, y, z} or nil
Where it last saw or heard its target, or nil.

The getters return whole numbers

GetSpeed, GetVisionRange and GetHearingRange return a plain number, the engine value with its fraction dropped: at the default GTE scaling an 8 m vision range (0.08 engine units) reads back as 0. Keep your own copy of a value you set.

docs.title: Patrol
docs.text:
Agent.AddWaypoint(actor, vec3)
Appends a patrol waypoint and turns patrolling on; the engine holds 8 and ignores more.

Agent.ClearWaypoints(actor)
Removes every waypoint and turns patrolling off.

Agent.SetPatrolEnabled(actor, bool)
Turns patrolling on or off; on, an Idle agent with waypoints switches to Patrol.

Agent events (onStateEnter, onTargetSeen, onPatrolPoint, ...) are listed under Events.

docs.title: Sprite
docs.text:
2D pictures cut from the scene's sprite sheets. Sheets and animations are authored in the editor; sprites are made here, at run time. A sprite is a plain number, its slot in a pool of 128: keep it in a variable or a table. Functions given an id that is not a live sprite do nothing (IsVisible returns false).

Pass names, not numbers

Sprite.Create, Sprite.PlayAnim and Sprite.SetFacingFromYaw take a sheet or animation name. They also mean to take an index, but the engine checks for a string first and Lua counts a number as a string, so Sprite.Create(0) looks for a sheet named "0" and returns -1. Always pass the name.

docs.title: Sheets and animations
docs.text:
Sprite.SheetIndex(name)  -- -> index or -1
The sheet's index in the scene, or -1 when no sheet has that name.

Sprite.AnimIndex(name)  -- -> index or -1
The animation's index, or -1 when none has that name. It searches every sheet and returns the first match, which is why the editor makes animation names unique across the scene.

docs.title: Creating and destroying
docs.text:
Sprite.Create(sheetName)  -- -> id or -1
Makes a sprite from a sheet and returns its id, 0 to 127. Returns -1 when the sheet does not exist or all 128 are in use. A new sprite is visible, on the screen plane at (0, 0), on layer 0, with a neutral tint, showing cell 0 and no animation.

Sprite.Destroy(id)
Frees the slot. The id may be handed out again by the next Create.

Sprite.Count()  -- -> number
How many sprites exist.

docs.title: Position
docs.text:
Sprite.SetPos(id, x, y)
Screen position of the sprite's top left corner, in whole pixels (-32768 to 32767).

Sprite.BindToActor(id, actor, plane, offsetX, offsetY)
Makes the sprite follow an object every frame. actor is an Actor.Find or Entity.Find handle; nil unbinds it. plane is 0 for the screen plane (the default) or 1 for the world plane; the offsets default to 0. On the screen plane the sprite's x is the object's X and its y the object's Z, in whole engine units, plus the offsets; the object's height is ignored. The bound position replaces whatever SetPos set.

Sprite.SetWorldPos(id, x, y, z)
Position on the world plane. The engine keeps it but does not draw world-plane sprites yet.

Sprite.SetViewOffset(x, y)
Sprite.GetViewOffset()  -- -> x, y
A scroll for every sprite at once, in pixels: each one is drawn at its position minus this offset. Starts at 0, 0.

Sprite.SetIgnoreViewOffset(id, bool)
True pins the sprite to the screen, ignoring the view offset (for a score or a cursor).

docs.title: Animation
docs.text:
Sprite.PlayAnim(id, animName, restart)
Plays an animation; the sprite switches to the animation's sheet. If the same animation is already playing it carries on, so calling this every frame is fine; pass true as restart to start it again from its first cell. An unknown name does nothing. Each cell shows for the animation's frame time in vsyncs, 60 a second of real time. A looping animation starts again after its last cell; otherwise it stops there.

Sprite.StopAnim(id)
Stops the animation on the cell it is showing.

Sprite.SetFrame(id, cell)
Shows one cell of the sprite's sheet, 0 to 255, counted row by row from the top left, and drops the animation. The cell is not checked against the sheet's size.

Sprite.SetFacingFromYaw(id, firstAnimName, directions, yaw)
For a character drawn from several directions: plays animation firstAnimName + n, where n (0 to directions - 1) is the direction nearest to yaw. The directional animations must follow one another in the sheet's list, starting with yaw 0 and going the way yaw increases. yaw is in pi-units like Entity.SetRotationY (1 = 180 degrees); yaw 0 is an object facing the same way as the camera, so pass the object's yaw minus Camera.GetRotation().y. The editor's Add direction set names them in this order, starting with _n. Changing direction keeps the cell and timing, so a walk cycle does not restart, and keeps whether it is playing: call PlayAnim first. directions of 0 does nothing.

docs.title: Look
docs.text:
Sprite.SetVisible(id, bool)
Sprite.IsVisible(id)  -- -> bool
Hides or shows the sprite.

Sprite.SetFlip(id, flipX, flipY)
Mirrors the picture left to right and/or top to bottom.

Sprite.SetColor(id, r, g, b)
Tints the sprite, each 0 to 255. 128, 128, 128 is the picture's own colours; higher brightens, up to double.

Sprite.SetSize(id, w, h)
Draws the cell stretched to w x h pixels. 0 for either keeps the cell's own width or height.

Sprite.SetLayer(id, layer)
Drawing order, 0 (front) to 11; a higher number is drawn as 11. All sprites are drawn in front of the 3D scene and behind UI canvases.

Unscaled sprites are cheapest

A sprite at its cell size and not flipped is drawn as a single GPU sprite. Flipping or a size other than the cell's makes it a textured quad.

docs.title: Tile
docs.text:
Questions to the scene's tilemap: what is walkable, and where its objects are. The map, its brushes and its objects are authored in the editor; Lua only reads them. Positions are whole pixels with the map's top left corner at 0, 0, x across the map and z down it: the same pixel space as the sprites, which a 2D game shares with the world X and Z of its actors. Off the map is not walkable.

Without a tilemap, Tile.Walkable, Tile.RayClear and Tile.MoveActor behave as if nothing were in the way, so movement written with them works in any scene.

docs.title: The map
docs.text:
Tile.Active()  -- -> bool
True when the scene has a tilemap.

Tile.MapSize()  -- -> width, height, tileW, tileH
The map's size in tiles and the tile size in pixels. All four are 0 without a map.

docs.title: Walls
docs.text:
Tile.Walkable(x, z)  -- -> bool
Whether the cell under pixel x, z is walkable. False off the map and on empty or hole cells; true when the scene has no tilemap.

Tile.RayClear(x0, z0, x1, z1)  -- -> bool
Whether the straight line between two pixels crosses only walkable cells, for line of sight. The first pixel's own cell is not tested; the last one's is, so a point inside a wall is not visible. The line is sampled every half tile (half the smaller tile side) and gives up after 128 samples: a longer line returns false. True without a tilemap.

Tile.MoveActor(actor, dx, dz, ignoreWalls)  -- -> x, z
Moves an actor (an Actor.Find or Actor.GetPlayer handle) by dx, dz pixels on its world X and Z, and returns where it ends up, in whole units. X is tried first, then Z, each on its own: a wall stops the move on that axis, so the actor slides along it. The actor's height is left alone. Pass true as ignoreWalls to move without looking at the map; without a tilemap the whole move is always made. Given something that is not an actor it returns a single null userdata, which is not nil.

docs.title: Objects
docs.text:
Tile.ObjectCount()  -- -> number
How many objects the map has, at most 128: one for each cell painted with a brush that has a kind, in reading order. 0 without a map.

Tile.ObjectAt(i)  -- -> kind, id, x, z
Object i, counted from 1: its kind, its id and the centre of its tile in pixels. Kinds and ids are the numbers set on the brush in the editor; the engine gives them no meaning.

Do not ask past the count

For an index outside 1 to Tile.ObjectCount(), ObjectAt returns a single value that is not nil (a null userdata), so if Tile.ObjectAt(i) then does not find the end. Loop with for i = 1, Tile.ObjectCount() do.

docs.title: Event Callbacks
docs.text:
All game logic is event-driven. You define callback functions in your Lua scripts, and the engine calls them when events happen.

The same events drive both kinds of script. In the block editor each event is a hat block; in Lua it is a function with the name below.

No game loop needed

You can build complex gameplay (dialogue, combat, puzzles, scene transitions) without ever using onUpdate. See Patterns for examples.

docs.title: Object Callbacks
docs.text: Defined in the script of an object's Script component. All receive self (the object) as the first argument.

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text:
function onCreate(self)
    -- Called once after the scene finishes loading and all objects are registered.
    -- Use for initialization. Entity.Find() works here for any object.
end

function onEnable(self)
    -- Called when Entity.SetActive(self, true) activates the object.
end

function onDisable(self)
    -- Called when Entity.SetActive(self, false) deactivates the object.
end

docs.title: Per-Frame
docs.text:
function onUpdate(self, dt)
    -- Called every frame. dt is a 4.12 fixed-point delta time value.
    -- 4096 = one 30fps frame (normal speed). Higher values mean the
    -- previous frame took longer (lag compensation). Capped at 4096*4.
    --
    -- Use sparingly. Every object with onUpdate runs this every frame.
    -- Prefer event-driven patterns instead.
end

docs.title: Player Interaction
docs.text:
function onCollideWithPlayer(self)
    -- Called when the player's collision capsule overlaps this object.
    -- Fires every frame while overlapping. Use a flag for one-time actions.
end

function onInteract(self)
    -- Called when the player presses the interact button while near this object.
    -- Needs an Interactable component on the same object.
end

docs.title: Input
docs.text:
function onButtonPress(self, button)
    -- Called on the frame a controller button is pressed (edge trigger).
    -- button is a number matching Input constants.
    -- Example: if button == Input.CROSS then ...
end

function onButtonRelease(self, button)
    -- Called on the frame a button is released.
end

Two players

These callbacks fire for presses on either controller and receive only the button id - not which player pressed it. To handle players separately, poll the Input.*Player1 / Input.*Player2 functions directly (typically in onUpdate).

docs.title: Scene Callbacks
docs.text:
Defined in the scene's own script (Script > File in the scene settings). No self argument.

function onSceneCreationStart()
    -- Called early in scene initialization, BEFORE objects are created.
    -- Good for: loading persistent data, initializing variables.
end

function onSceneCreationEnd()
    -- Called AFTER all objects are created and their onCreate() has fired.
    -- Good for: UI setup, starting ambient effects, initial game state.
end

docs.title: Agent Callbacks
docs.text:
Defined in the script of an object with an Agent (NPC) component (see Agents). States are the numbers Agent.GetState returns.

function onStateEnter(self, newState, oldState)
    -- Called after the agent's state changes (Agent.SetState, or Idle -> Patrol on its own).
end

function onStateExit(self, state)
    -- Called just before it leaves `state`.
end

function onTargetSeen(self, target)
    -- Called when it starts seeing its target (the player unless Agent.SetTarget set another).
    -- target is nil for the player.
end

function onTargetLost(self, target)
    -- Called once the alert timeout runs out after it last saw or heard the target.
end

function onTargetReached(self)
    -- Called when it arrives at a position in the Seek, Wander or Investigate state
    -- (not while following an actor).
end

function onPatrolPoint(self, index)
    -- Called at each patrol waypoint, index counting from 0.
end

function onPathBlocked(self)
    -- Registered, but the engine never calls it yet.
end

docs.title: Trigger Callbacks
docs.text:
Defined in the script of a Trigger box component. No self argument: the one argument is index, the trigger's index in the scene.

function onTriggerEnter(index)
    -- Called when the player enters the trigger volume.
end

function onTriggerExit(index)
    -- Called when the player leaves the trigger volume.
end

docs.title: Callback Execution Order
docs.text:
On scene load, callbacks fire in this order:

  1. onSceneCreationStart() (scene script)
  2. Scene Lua file executes (top-level code runs)
  3. onCreate(self) for all objects (after ALL objects are registered, so Entity.Find works)
  4. onSceneCreationEnd() (scene script)

During gameplay, per frame:

  1. Cutscenes, animations and skinned meshes tick -> onComplete callbacks
  2. Player movement and collision -> onCollideWithPlayer, onTriggerEnter / onTriggerExit
  3. onUpdate(self, dt) for each active object with the callback
  4. Enable/disable events batched and fired -> onEnable, onDisable
  5. Controller state updated -> onInteract, then onButtonPress / onButtonRelease
  6. Navigation mesh update

Collision runs before onUpdate, not after

A position you write in onUpdate is not collision-checked until the next frame.

docs.title: Event Optimization
docs.text:
The engine scans each script for which callbacks are defined and sets a bitmask. Scripts that don't define a callback never get checked for that event. This means:

  • An object without onUpdate has zero per-frame cost
  • An object without onCollideWithPlayer is never collision-checked
  • Only define the callbacks you actually need

docs.title: Fixed-Point Math
docs.text: This is the most important page if you are writing Lua for psxsplash. The PS1 has no floating-point unit, so all math uses fixed-point integers.

docs.title: The Rules
docs.text:
1. Never write decimal literals. 0.5, 1.5, 3.14 - none of these work.
  2. Plain integer division does NOT give you fractions. 1/2 equals 0, not 0.5. This is integer division.
  3. Use FixedPoint.new() for ALL fractional values. This is the only way to create non-integer numbers.
  4. All API functions accept and return fixed-point numbers. Positions, rotations, distances - everything.

docs.title: How It Works
docs.text:
Numbers in psxsplash Lua are 20.12 fixed-point integers:

  • 20 bits for the integer part
  • 12 bits for the fractional part
  • Scale factor: 4096 (4096 = 1.0 internally)
  • Range: approximately -524288 to +524287

You don't need to think about the internal representation. Just follow the rules above.

docs.title: Creating Fractional Values
docs.text:
The only way to get a fractional value is through FixedPoint.new():

-- Create a FixedPoint value and divide it
local one = FixedPoint.new(1)
local half = one / 2              -- 0.5
local quarter = one / 4           -- 0.25
local threeQuarters = one * 3 / 4 -- 0.75
local step = one / 64             -- ~0.015625
local small = one / 16            -- 0.0625

Common Mistake

-- WRONG: These all equal 0!
local half = 1/2        -- Integer division: 0
local frac = 5/4        -- Integer division: 1
local tiny = 1/64       -- Integer division: 0
local bad = 0.5         -- Float literal: doesn't work

-- CORRECT: Use FixedPoint.new()
local one = FixedPoint.new(1)
local half = one / 2    -- Proper fixed-point 0.5
local frac = one * 5 / 4  -- Proper fixed-point 1.25
local tiny = one / 64   -- Proper fixed-point ~0.016

docs.title: Whole Numbers Are Fine
docs.text:
Plain integers work as-is for whole numbers:

local ten = 10          -- This is fine
local zero = 0          -- This is fine
local big = 1000        -- This is fine

You only need FixedPoint.new() when you need a value with a fractional part.

docs.title: Rotation Values
docs.text:
Rotations use pi-units: 1024 internal units = pi radians = 180 degrees.

Angle Lua Value How to Write 0 0 0 45 degrees 0.25 pi FixedPoint.new(1) / 4 90 degrees 0.5 pi FixedPoint.new(1) / 2 180 degrees 1 pi 1 270 degrees 1.5 pi FixedPoint.new(3) / 2 360 degrees 2 pi 2 
local one = FixedPoint.new(1)

-- Rotate 90 degrees
Entity.SetRotationY(self, one / 2)

-- Add 180 degrees to current rotation (1 is a whole number, fine as-is)
local rot = Entity.GetRotationY(self)
Entity.SetRotationY(self, rot + 1)

-- Small rotation
Entity.SetRotationY(self, rot + one / 64)

docs.title: Math Functions
docs.text:
Math functions work with fixed-point numbers. Remember to use FixedPoint.new() for fractional arguments:

local one = FixedPoint.new(1)

-- PSXMath utilities
local clamped = PSXMath.Clamp(value, 0, 100)
local lerped = PSXMath.Lerp(0, 10, one / 2)   -- Interpolate halfway: result is 5
local sign = PSXMath.Sign(-42)                  -- Result: -1
local abs = PSXMath.Abs(-7)                     -- Result: 7

docs.title: Vec3 Operations
docs.text:
Vectors are tables with x, y, z fields. Fractional components require FixedPoint:

local one = FixedPoint.new(1)

local pos = Vec3.new(10, 0, 5)
local dir = Vec3.new(one / 2, 0, one / 2)

local sum = Vec3.add(pos, dir)
local dist = Vec3.distance(pos, Vec3.new(0, 0, 0))

docs.title: String Concatenation
docs.text:
FixedPoint values work with the .. string operator:

local pos = self.position
Debug.Log("Position: " .. pos.x .. ", " .. pos.y .. ", " .. pos.z)

docs.title: Common Gotchas
docs.text:
onUpdate dt is fixed-point

The dt parameter passed to onUpdate(self, dt) is a 4.12 fixed-point value where 4096 = one 30fps frame. To scale a movement by dt: local scaled = step * dt / 4096.

Integer division is silent

1/2 silently evaluates to 0. There's no error, no warning. Your code runs, but with wrong values. Always use FixedPoint.new() for fractions.

Integer overflow

Very large multiplications can overflow the 32-bit fixed-point range. Keep intermediate values reasonable.

Reuse your FixedPoint local

Create local one = FixedPoint.new(1) once at the top of your script or function, then derive all fractions from it. Don't call FixedPoint.new() inside hot loops.

docs.title: Patterns & Best Practices
docs.text: Working code patterns for common game mechanics, with tested examples.

docs.title: Core Pattern: Event-Driven Design
docs.text:
Scripts stay small and fast when they react to events instead of polling:

  • onInteract for player-initiated actions
  • onButtonPress for button-driven controls
  • onCollideWithPlayer for collision responses
  • onTriggerEnter / onTriggerExit for area triggers
  • Animation.Play with callbacks for time-based actions
  • Cutscene.Play with callbacks for sequenced events

docs.title: Core Pattern: Scene as Controller
docs.text:
The scene script is the central coordinator. Define shared functions there and publish them to _G so object scripts can access them:

-- the scene script

local score = 0
local scoreText = -1

function onSceneCreationEnd()
    local hud = UI.FindCanvas("HUD")
    scoreText = UI.FindElement(hud, "ScoreText")
end

function addScore(amount)
    score = score + amount
    if scoreText >= 0 then
        UI.SetText(scoreText, "Score: " .. score)
    end
end

function setStatus(msg)
    Debug.Log("[Status] " .. msg)
end

-- CRITICAL: Publish to _G so object scripts can call these
_G.addScore = addScore
_G.setStatus = setStatus

Object scripts call these directly:

-- a pickup object script
function onCollideWithPlayer(self)
    addScore(100)
    setStatus("Got it!")
end

docs.title: Pattern: One-Time Action
docs.text:
Use a local flag to prevent repeated triggers:

local collected = false

function onCollideWithPlayer(self)
    if collected then return end
    collected = true

    Audio.Play("collect", 127, 64)
    Entity.SetActive(self, false)
    addScore(100)
    setStatus("Collected! +100 points")
end

docs.title: Pattern: Animation Gating
docs.text:
Prevent overlapping animations by checking IsPlaying before starting:

local isOpen = false

function onInteract(self)
    -- Don't start if either animation is running
    if Animation.IsPlaying("door_open") or Animation.IsPlaying("door_close") then
        return
    end

    -- Disable interaction during animation
    Interact.SetEnabled(self, false)

    if isOpen then
        isOpen = false
        Audio.Play("door_close", 100, 64)
        Animation.Play("door_close", {
            onComplete = function()
                Interact.SetEnabled(self, true)
            end
        })
    else
        isOpen = true
        Audio.Play("door_open", 100, 64)
        Animation.Play("door_open", {
            onComplete = function()
                Interact.SetEnabled(self, true)
            end
        })
    end
end

docs.title: Pattern: Dialogue System
docs.text: Build a dialogue system in the scene script, then call it from NPC scripts:

docs.title: Scene Script (Dialogue System)
docs.text:
-- the scene script
local dialogueCanvas = -1
local dialogueText = -1
local inDialogue = false
local dialogueLines = {}
local dialogueLine = 0

function onSceneCreationEnd()
    dialogueCanvas = UI.FindCanvas("Dialogue")
    if dialogueCanvas >= 0 then
        dialogueText = UI.FindElement(dialogueCanvas, "DialogueText")
        UI.SetCanvasVisible(dialogueCanvas, false)
    end
end

function startDialogue(lines)
    if inDialogue then return end
    inDialogue = true
    dialogueLines = lines
    dialogueLine = 1
    Controls.SetEnabledPlayer1(false)
    UI.SetCanvasVisible(dialogueCanvas, true)
    UI.SetText(dialogueText, dialogueLines[1])
end

function advanceDialogue()
    if not inDialogue then return end
    dialogueLine = dialogueLine + 1
    if dialogueLine > #dialogueLines then
        endDialogue()
    else
        UI.SetText(dialogueText, dialogueLines[dialogueLine])
    end
end

function endDialogue()
    inDialogue = false
    Controls.SetEnabledPlayer1(true)
    UI.SetCanvasVisible(dialogueCanvas, false)
end

function isInDialogue()
    return inDialogue
end

-- Publish all
_G.startDialogue = startDialogue
_G.advanceDialogue = advanceDialogue
_G.endDialogue = endDialogue
_G.isInDialogue = isInDialogue

docs.title: NPC Script
docs.text:
-- an NPC object script
local talked = false

function onCreate(self)
    talked = false
end

function onInteract(self)
    if isInDialogue() then return end
    Interact.SetEnabled(self, false)

    if not talked then
        talked = true
        startDialogue({
            "Hello, traveler!",
            "Welcome to the world.",
            "Press CROSS to continue."
        })
    else
        startDialogue({
            "Hello again!",
            "Nothing new to say."
        })
    end
end

function onButtonPress(self, button)
    if not isInDialogue() then return end
    if button == Input.CROSS then
        advanceDialogue()
        if not isInDialogue() then
            Interact.SetEnabled(self, true)
        end
    end
end

docs.title: Pattern: Persistent Data Across Scenes
docs.text:
Use Persist to carry data between scene loads:

-- Before leaving the scene
Persist.Set("score", currentScore)
Persist.Set("health", currentHealth)
Persist.Set("came_from", Scene.GetIndex())
Scene.Load(1)

-- In the new scene
function onSceneCreationStart()
    local score = Persist.Get("score") or 0
    local health = Persist.Get("health") or 100
    local prevScene = Persist.Get("came_from") or -1
    Debug.Log("Arrived from scene " .. prevScene)
end

16 entry limit

Persist supports only 16 key-value pairs. Use it for important game state only.

docs.title: Pattern: Toggle Switch
docs.text:
Control another object by name lookup:

local target = nil
local isOn = false

function onCreate(self)
    target = Entity.Find("SwitchTarget")
    if target then
        Entity.SetActive(target, false)
    else
        Debug.Log("WARNING: SwitchTarget not found!")
    end
end

function onInteract(self)
    isOn = not isOn
    if target then
        Entity.SetActive(target, isOn)
    end
    Audio.Play(isOn and "switch_on" or "switch_off", 100, 64)
    setStatus(isOn and "Switch ON" or "Switch OFF")
end

docs.title: Pattern: Object Movement with Buttons
docs.text:
Move objects using button input with fixed-point step sizes:

local selected = false

function onInteract(self)
    selected = not selected
    if selected then
        Controls.SetEnabledPlayer1(false)
        Interact.SetEnabled(self, false)
        setStatus("D-pad to move, L1/R1 for height, Triangle to deselect")
    else
        Controls.SetEnabledPlayer1(true)
        Interact.SetEnabled(self, true)
    end
end

function onButtonPress(self, button)
    if not selected then return end

    local pos = self.position
    local step = FixedPoint.new(1) / 64

    if button == Input.UP then
        Entity.SetPosition(self, Vec3.new(pos.x, pos.y, pos.z + step))
    elseif button == Input.DOWN then
        Entity.SetPosition(self, Vec3.new(pos.x, pos.y, pos.z - step))
    elseif button == Input.LEFT then
        Entity.SetPosition(self, Vec3.new(pos.x - step, pos.y, pos.z))
    elseif button == Input.RIGHT then
        Entity.SetPosition(self, Vec3.new(pos.x + step, pos.y, pos.z))
    elseif button == Input.L1 then
        Entity.SetPosition(self, Vec3.new(pos.x, pos.y + step, pos.z))
    elseif button == Input.R1 then
        Entity.SetPosition(self, Vec3.new(pos.x, pos.y - step, pos.z))
    elseif button == Input.SQUARE then
        local rot = Entity.GetRotationY(self)
        local one = FixedPoint.new(1)
        Entity.SetRotationY(self, rot + one / 2)  -- Rotate 90 degrees
    elseif button == Input.TRIANGLE then
        selected = false
        Controls.SetEnabledPlayer1(true)
        Interact.SetEnabled(self, true)
    end
end

docs.title: Pattern: Lua Free Cam
docs.text:
Disclaimer: onUpdate runs every frame so you can very easily lag out your project if you start using it for everything.

Only use onUpdate if you really need to. This example script just demonstrates how you would make a smooth free cam but you could also modify it to have the camera jump to the next position/rotation in a large step with each button press and completely remove onUpdate.

dt is fixed-point

The dt parameter is a 4.12 fixed-point delta time (4096 = one 30fps frame). You can multiply movement values by dt / 4096 for frame-rate-independent motion, though at a fixed 30fps target it's usually fine to ignore it.

-- Example Lua Free Cam --
-- Author: Latch
--
-- This script allows you to fully control the camera
-- with lua. You can also save the camera position+rotation
-- with square, move the camera somewhere else, and then
-- use circle to load the saved position+rotation
--
-- Warning!
-- the Player will overwrite these values
--

local camRotStep = FixedPoint.new(1) / 128
local camMoveStep = FixedPoint.new(1) / 1024

local savedCamRotation = Vec3.new(0,0,0)
local savedCamPosition = Vec3.new(0,0,0)

function onCreate(self)
    -- Make sure we have control of the camera
    Camera.FollowPsxPlayer(false)
end

function onUpdate(self, dt)

    local camPos = Camera.GetPosition()

    -- Camera Movement
    if Input.IsHeldPlayer1(Input.UP) then
        Camera.MoveForward(camMoveStep)
    elseif Input.IsHeldPlayer1(Input.DOWN) then
        Camera.MoveBackward(camMoveStep)
    elseif Input.IsHeldPlayer1(Input.LEFT) then
        Camera.MoveLeft(camMoveStep)
    elseif Input.IsHeldPlayer1(Input.RIGHT) then
        Camera.MoveRight(camMoveStep)
    elseif Input.IsHeldPlayer1(Input.TRIANGLE) then
        Camera.SetPosition(Vec3.new(camPos.x,camPos.y-camMoveStep,camPos.z))
    elseif Input.IsHeldPlayer1(Input.CROSS) then
        Camera.SetPosition(Vec3.new(camPos.x,camPos.y+camMoveStep,camPos.z))

    end

    local camRot = Camera.GetRotation()

    -- Camera Rotation
    if Input.IsHeldPlayer1(Input.L1) then
        Camera.SetRotation(Vec3.new(camRot.x,camRot.y-camRotStep,camRot.z))   
    elseif Input.IsHeldPlayer1(Input.R1) then
        Camera.SetRotation(Vec3.new(camRot.x,camRot.y+camRotStep,camRot.z))
    elseif Input.IsHeldPlayer1(Input.L2) then
        Camera.SetRotation(Vec3.new(camRot.x-camRotStep,camRot.y,camRot.z)) 
    elseif Input.IsHeldPlayer1(Input.R2) then
        Camera.SetRotation(Vec3.new(camRot.x+camRotStep,camRot.y,camRot.z))
    end
end

function onButtonPress(self, button)

    -- Camera Saving And Loading
    if button == Input.SQUARE then
        Debug.Log("Saving cam position and rotation")
        savedCamPosition = Camera.GetPosition()        
        savedCamRotation = Camera.GetRotation()
    elseif button == Input.CIRCLE then
        Debug.Log("Loading saved position and rotation")
        Camera.SetPosition(savedCamPosition);
        Camera.SetRotation(savedCamRotation);
    end
end

docs.title: Pattern: Health System
docs.text:
Color-coded health bar with damage and healing:

-- the scene script
local health = 100
local healthBar = -1

function onSceneCreationEnd()
    local hud = UI.FindCanvas("HUD")
    healthBar = UI.FindElement(hud, "HealthBar")
    updateHealthBar()
end

function updateHealthBar()
    if healthBar < 0 then return end
    UI.SetProgress(healthBar, health)

    if health > 50 then
        UI.SetProgressColors(healthBar, 0, 40, 0, 0, 255, 0)        -- Green
    elseif health > 25 then
        UI.SetProgressColors(healthBar, 40, 40, 0, 255, 255, 0)     -- Yellow
    else
        UI.SetProgressColors(healthBar, 40, 0, 0, 255, 0, 0)        -- Red
    end
end

function applyDamage(amount)
    health = PSXMath.Clamp(health - amount, 0, 100)
    updateHealthBar()
    if health <= 0 then
        setStatus("You died! Reloading...")
        Controls.SetEnabledPlayer1(false)
        Persist.Set("score", 0)
        Scene.Load(Scene.GetIndex())  -- Reload current scene
    end
end

function applyHeal(amount)
    health = PSXMath.Clamp(health + amount, 0, 100)
    updateHealthBar()
end

_G.applyDamage = applyDamage
_G.applyHeal = applyHeal

docs.title: Nightly editor
docs.text:
The editor, engine and emulator ship as one download, rebuilt from every change to the editor's main branch. Download.

  • A standalone editor for Windows, Linux and macOS (Apple silicon) with a PS1-accurate viewport, scene tree, inspector, project browser and live VRAM, SPU RAM and main RAM meters.
  • Play boots the scene in the bundled pcsx-redux next to the viewport and reloads it as you edit. Run on hardware sends it to a console over serial with Unirom. Export writes a .bin and .cue disc image.
  • A Lua editor with highlighting, a compile check, autocomplete with signatures, go to definition and find and replace.
  • A block editor that makes Lua from stacks of blocks. Blocks and Lua can be mixed in one scene.
  • UI canvases, cutscenes and animations on a timeline, skinned animation, rooms and portals, audio clips, runtime point lights and world streaming.
  • Model import for glTF, FBX, OBJ and Blender files, with per-model import settings and a texture bit depth check that offers 4 bpp.
  • Memory card save settings, disc volume label and licence options, and a loading screen canvas.
  • Lua: Light functions, SkinnedAnim.GetBone, and Camera.LookAt now points the camera at its target.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: Terms used in these docs that assume PS1 background.

docs.title: OT (Ordering Table)
docs.text: A fixed-size array of depth buckets the GPU primitives are linked into before they are sent to the GPU. The PS1 has no Z-buffer, so this is how depth sorting works. The slot count is also how far the camera sees. See Render buffers.

docs.title: GTE (Geometry Transformation Engine)
docs.text: The PS1 CPU's coprocessor 2, a fixed-function unit that does matrix and vector math (transforms, projection, lighting) in hardware. Its coordinates are 16-bit fixed point, which is why exported positions are divided by the scene's GTE scaling and must sit within 8 x the scaling of the origin. See Rendering.

docs.title: Fixed-point
docs.text: Numbers stored as integers with an implied binary point. psxsplash Lua uses 20.12: 4096 is 1.0. See Fixed-Point Math.

docs.title: Splashpack
docs.text: The binary file the editor exports a scene into (scene_0.splashpack). The psxsplash engine reads it to load a scene's objects, meshes, navigation, UI and scripts. Textures go in a .vram file beside it and audio in a .spu file.

docs.title: Bump allocator
docs.text: A per-frame allocator that resets every frame, used for the GPU command buffer. The editor calls it the Primitive buffer.

docs.title: VRAM
docs.text: The GPU's own 1 MB, addressed as 1024 x 512 pixels of 16 bits. Framebuffers, textures, palettes and the font live here.

docs.title: CLUT (Color Look-Up Table)
docs.text: A palette stored in VRAM that 4 bpp and 8 bpp textures point into: 16 or 256 entries of 16-bit colour.

docs.title: SPU (Sound Processing Unit)
docs.text: The PS1's audio chip, with 512 KB of its own RAM and 24 ADPCM voices.

docs.title: PCdrv
docs.text: A debug-link facility that lets the PS1 read files from the host computer as a virtual drive. Play and Run on hardware use it to serve the exported scene files, so nothing needs burning.

docs.title: Unirom
docs.text: A PS1 boot ROM and shell that accepts programs over the serial port. Run on hardware needs it.

docs.title: Room and portal
docs.text: A Room is a box of static geometry that draws only when it can be seen. A Portal is the opening between two Rooms the camera can see through. See Rooms and portals.

docs.title: BVH
docs.text: A tree of bounding boxes over the scene's triangles. Without Rooms, the engine draws only triangles in boxes the camera sees.

docs.title: Known Issues
docs.text: What does not work yet, or works differently than you would guess. Each item was checked against the current editor and engine source.

docs.title: The engine never calls onDestroy
docs.text: Lua::OnDestroy exists in psxsplash, but nothing calls it, and no Lua function destroys an object. Objects go away when the scene is cleared, and clearing calls no callback, so a Lua onDestroy never runs. Use Entity.SetActive(object, false) and onDisable.

docs.title: Debug.DrawLine and Debug.DrawBox draw nothing
docs.text: Both accept their arguments and return, but neither queues a primitive. Calls are harmless. UI.DrawLine and UI.DrawTriangle do draw.

docs.title: Camera control is taken back by the player
docs.text: In a scene with a Player and a nav mesh, the player controller overrides the camera every frame. Call Camera.FollowPsxPlayer(false) before moving the camera from Lua. Cutscenes suspend the controller by themselves.

docs.title: Persist holds 16 numbers
docs.text: Setting more silently fails. Use the memory card API for larger or longer-lived state.

docs.title: Controller rumble has no Lua API
docs.text: The motors can be driven by Rumble tracks in the timeline, not from a script.

docs.title: The inspector cannot set a light to runtime
docs.text: Runtime point lights exist in the engine, the Light API and timeline tracks, but the Light component has no switch for them; set "runtime": true in the scene file. See Lighting.

docs.title: Fonts and finer nav settings live in the scene file
docs.text: The UI tab picks from the scene's fonts but does not add them, and the nav bake's cell size and region merging keep their defaults unless you edit the scene file.

docs.title: No network link in the editor
docs.text: The engine has a Net table, but the editor has no way to author a network link yet, so it is not in these docs.

docs.title: Scene type is stored but not used
docs.text: Exterior and Interior change nothing. Culling follows the Room objects.

docs.title: A dynamic collider does not rotate
docs.text: Rotating an object from Lua does not recalculate its collision box. Position changes do.

docs.title: No CD-DA from the editor
docs.text: The disc images the editor writes have one data track, and Play and Run on hardware use PCdrv. Audio.PlayCDDA has nothing to play. Use audio clips.

docs.title: Platform
docs.text:
• Windows: the executable is not signed. SmartScreen stops the first launch: More info, then Run anyway.
  • macOS: Apple silicon only, and the app is not notarized. Clear the quarantine once; see Installation.
  • Linux: needs glibc 2.38 or newer.

docs.title: Reporting
docs.text: Found one that is not listed? Help > Report a Problem opens the issue tracker.

docs.title: Memory & Performance
docs.text: The PS1 has little of everything, and psxsplash games run into the same walls. The editor shows where you stand against each wall while you work.

docs.title: Hardware limits
docs.text: Resource Limit Main RAM 2 MB, shared by engine, scene data, render buffers and the Lua VM VRAM 1 MB (1024 x 512 at 16 bits) SPU RAM 512 KB of audio CPU 33 MHz MIPS R3000A, no FPU SPU voices 24 at once

docs.title: The status bar meters
docs.text:
At the bottom of the editor, for the scene as it would export right now:

Meter Counts VRAM Out of 1024 KB: two 320 x 240 framebuffers, the font column, texture atlases and their palettes (CLUTs) SPU RAM Out of 512 KB: your audio clips RAM Main RAM left for the scene after the engine: scene data, render buffers, streaming slots, and a per-object cost Triangles Triangles in the scene (not the number visible at once)

The numbers come from the same export Play uses, so they follow every edit. The scene settings show where textures sit in VRAM.

docs.title: Where main RAM goes
docs.text:
• Scene data: objects, meshes, collision, navigation, UI, cutscenes, animations, skinned clips, Lua bytecode.
  • Render buffers: two ordering tables and two primitive buffers, sized from the scene. See Render buffers.
  • Per object: every object costs RAM at load whether or not it has a script: a few hundred bytes for its runtime state, plus two Lua tables. A scene of a thousand-plus objects can run out of RAM on that alone. The editor warns Too many objects for RAM and can select the biggest group. Merging objects (the Merge meshes import setting) fixes it.
  • Streaming slots, when world streaming is on.
  • Lua VM and engine state.

docs.title: Fixed pools
docs.text:
The engine reserves fixed-size pools for these, which is also why the editor enforces the limits:

Pool Size UI canvases 24 UI elements 256 across the scene Cutscenes 16 per scene, 8 tracks each Animations 8 playing at once Rooms 31 per scene Runtime lights 16 per scene, 4 per mesh Persist entries 16 numbers

docs.title: Textures (VRAM)
docs.text:
1. Use 4 bpp when the texture allows. The inspector offers it when a texture has 16 colours or fewer. See Materials & Bit Depth.
  2. Keep textures small. 64 x 64 and 128 x 128 are normal PS1 sizes; 256 x 256 is the maximum.
  3. Reuse textures. Each distinct texture takes VRAM.

docs.title: Geometry
docs.text:
1. Use rooms and portals for indoor scenes, so only visible rooms are drawn. See Rooms and portals.
  2. Use fog to shorten how far the console draws.
  3. Watch the primitive buffer. If a frame needs more than it holds, the game stops with "Out of memory". The settings show the busiest frame under Play.
  4. Check FPS with Build > Performance Overlay.

docs.title: Skinned meshes (RAM)
docs.text: Each frame of each clip stores 24 bytes per bone. Fewer bones, shorter clips and a lower Bake rate all shrink it. The inspector's Baked block lists the size of every clip.

docs.title: Audio (SPU RAM)
docs.text: ADPCM takes about 0.57 bytes per sample, so a 5-second clip at 22050 Hz is about 63 KB. Lower the Sample rate, keep clips short, and plan for 24 voices at most.

docs.title: Lua (RAM and CPU)
docs.text:
1. React to events instead of polling. onUpdate runs every frame for every object that defines it.
  2. Define only the callbacks you use. The engine checks a bitmask; undefined callbacks cost nothing.
  3. Persist holds 16 numbers. For anything larger or longer-lived, use the memory card API.
